            Task 3: Master Plan
            The FFF Team will build from the Heights District Plan’s development and programmatic elements supporting
            the internal and external street network and collection of public use areas through an iterative process of
            preliminary concepts development, identification of necessary refinements and concepts review to create a
            preferred concept for the Heights District’s network of street and public uses areas. The product of Task 3 will
            be 1). a comprehensive Field Guide, establishing the base condition with technical analyses of the Adopted
            Heights District Plan and supporting polices and regulations and 2). A Place Guide including a preferred
            concept, supporting cost estimating, phasing, and supporting plans and strategies that establishes the
            framework for Task 4 Design Development Documentation and preparation of the 30% Design submittal
                           Field Guide
            The First Forty Feet Consultant team will obtain, assess, and review Project area background information and
            drawings including, but not limited to the Heights District Plan, Heights District Plan Appendices, Heights Final
            Planned Action Environmental Impact Statement, Draft Heights Plan District (HX Zone) regulations, Heights
            District Draft Urban Design Guidelines and other plans, standards, guidelines or documents identified and
            deemed necessary by the COV.

            First Forty Feet team will create a Field Guide document consisting of a preliminary site plan drawing, and
            summary report of the Project limits (Appendix A) design criteria (guidelines and standards) and programming
            for public use areas, streets and rights of way. The Field Guide enables the Project Team to confirm the design
            intentions of the Heights District Plan, assess and evaluate existing conditions, including planned and in-
            process infrastructure improvements and identify areas for possible plan adjustments, modifications or
            deviations. The Field Guide will establish the base condition for developing preliminary concepts and
            alternatives and a preferred concept plan that will be taken to 30% Design. The Field Guide will consist of the
            following elements:

            Subtask 3.1.1 Project Guidelines, Standards, and Program Elements
            The FFF Team will prepare a summary of the Heights District Project design guidelines, standards, and
            program elements for the Project area in excel spreadsheet and/or plan diagram exhibits for COV staff
            concurrence. Guidelines, standards and program elements will include but not be limited to:
                •    Heights District streets: including rights-of-way, typical street sections, and plans for E. Mill Plain
                     Boulevard, MacArthur Boulevard, N. Devine Road (Mill Plain Boulevard to MacArthur Boulevard, N.
                     Devine Road (Southeast Idaho Avenue to East 18th Street), N. Andresen Road, and , East McLoughlin
                     Area Safety Improvement Project
                •    Tower Mall Redevelopment Area internal streets: adopted Plan rights-of-way and typical street sections
                     consisting of the Loop Street (retail, residential, and festival street segments), Standard Street, and
                     Internal Street
                •    Planned round-a-bouts: including conceptual drawing plans and sections for RAB’s at N Devine Road
                     and N Andresen Road
                •    Planned BRT Stations: as-built drawing plans and sections for stations at E. Mill Plain Boulevard and N.
                     Devine Road and at E. Mill Plain Boulevard and N. Andresen Road.

                •    Public realm and open space: guidelines for the area (AC), location, program elements, and use

                •    Public Art and Wayfinding: guidelines for art and signage location, art features (representing culture,

            Subtask 3.1.2 Project Preliminary Base Map
            FFF and PBS will develop a preliminary base map of the Project area inclusive of planned projects identified by
            the COV affecting the Project area. The FFF Team will compile a comprehensive list of base data to be
            provided by the COV map (readily available plans, drawings, GIS, and CAD files) that is necessary to develop a
            preliminary base.

            The preliminary base map is intended to establish the base condition for streets, transit facilities, Cemetery
            trails and public use areas (Civic Park, Neighborhood Park and Pocket Parks) within the Project limits and will
            be updated as needed and based on PBS completion of the topographic/existing conditions survey and
            development of the surface model. A boundary resolution and topographic/existing conditions base map
            showing mapped features and utilities collected from both field survey and as-built plans will be prepared as
            indicated in Task 4.

            Subtask 3.1.3: Adopted Heights District Plan: Preferred Concept Plan Assessment and Evaluation
            FFF will prepare an assessment and evaluation of the retail components of the activity center, civic park/plaza,
            neighborhood park and internal street alignments based on the criteria and fundamental characteristics for
            supporting retail, active public use areas and maximizing development potential within the Tower Mall
            Redevelopment Area. FFF criteria and fundamental characteristics will consider:
                •    Edge-to-edge retail configuration on both sides of the retail street
                •    Adequate drive-by traffic (5,000-15,000 ADT), visibility, and direct retail access
                •    Retail street design with on-street parking, bicycle access and parking, wide sidewalks to support
                     through pedestrian movement, retail display, outdoor seating and furnishings.
                •    Plaza activated on all sides, highly visible and directly accessible from surrounding streets
                •    Potential access and easement issues with the internal streets layout and impacts on private parcels.

            The FFF Team will identify issues, possible challenges and recommendations for potential modifications to be
            addressed with COV in a Heights Project Field Guide Work Session.

            Subtask 3.1.4 Field Guide Document
            First Forty Feet team will create a Field Guide document consisting of a site plan drawing (preliminary base
            map), and summary report of the Project limits design criteria and programming for public use areas, streets
            and rights of way (Subtasks 4.1.1-4.1.3) The Field Guide will establish the base condition for developing
            preliminary concepts and alternatives and a preferred concept plan that will be taken to 30% Design.

            The work session is intended to:
                         o     Confirm placemaking features to be considered, including the Civic Building, interim
                               programming for public area activation, public art integration and wayfinding

            developed that meets appropriate design standards. Consultant shall prepare a drawing stamped
            “preliminary” for each concept. The drawing shall utilize the consultant provided ortho-rectified drone aerial
            imagery, topographic survey, GIS boundary and environmental data. Geometric design elements that do not
            meet design standards shall be identified as needing a design exception. Consultant shall analyze each
            concept and determine the potential benefits and impacts associated with construction of the proposed
            concept. Potential benefits and impacts to be considered include, but are not limited to, right-of-way, safety,
            utilities, construction costs, permitting and environmental Impacts.

            Subtask 3.4.1 Infrastructure Funding Opportunities
            LCG will lead this task, with input from FFF Team and the COV.

                     Management, other team members. The City may provide input.

                     and operations at the Heights. LCG will facilitate one or two team meetings to brainstorm potential
                     funding sources and assign specific research to different team members. For example, PBS is already
                     aware of a number of specific funding opportunities for transportation infrastructure. LCG and the team
                     will generate potential funding sources for the following plan elements:
                          o     Capital Improvements
                                   § Streets
                                   § Water
                                   § Sewer
                                   § Land Acquisitions
                                   § Stormwater improvements serving streets and private development
                                   § Parks
                          o     Operations of the parks and/or district. (This analysis will not evaluate funding sources for the
                                operations of water, sewer, or other public utilities.)
                •    LCG and the FFF team will document the potential to secure funds from:
                          o     Land sales or leases
                          o     Infrastructure built by developers/property owners
                          o     Impact fees dedicated to the site
                          o     District-scale funding sources such as tax increment financing (TIF), local improvement
                                districts (LID), and Business Improvement Districts (BID).
                          o     City sources such as Capital Improvement Plans
                          o     SW Washington Regional Transportation Council, e.g., Transportation Alternatives grants
                          o     Existing special districts, if any
                          o     State grants such as Transportation Improvement Board (TIB), Ecology, and others TBD.
                          o     Federal grants such as RAISE or BUILD grants.
                •    For each funding source, LCG and/or other team members will document:
                          o     The types of projects funded by the source
                          o     Approximate amount of likely funding, which may be based on past allocations.
                          o     Funding criteria
                          o     Web site and/or contact information
                          o     Other information.

                          Utility Coordination
            Franchise Utility Coordination
            PBS will contact franchise utilities within the project limits and obtain existing system mapping and discuss
            service requirements for the redeveloped Heights District.

            A utility reconnaissance of the project corridor will be conducted to determine visual evidence of
            underground and aboveground utility facilities and confirm utility provided facility maps and project base
            map completeness.

            Clark Public Utilities
            Consultant will meet with Clark Public Utilities to review power service capacity for the redeveloped Heights
            District, potential power demand, power infrastructure improvements, and location of substations. Potential
            phasing of improvements will be discussed and potential uses that would necessitate facility upgrades will be
            evaluated. Building sizes and uses will be required to finalize system impacts and requirements, but
            conceptual level discussions will be based on the adopted Master Plan. The Consultant will also explore the
            possibility and location of joint utility trenches to facilitate service for multiple franchise utilities into the
            Heights District. Meetings will also discuss opportunities to extend power into the Heights District while
            keeping service to the existing buildings and strategies for retrofitting power service as proposed blocks
            redevelop.

            Cable/Phone Utilities
            Consultant will meet with providers of Cable and Telephone utilities to discuss existing service into the
            Heights District and requirement to provide high speed Cable and Phone service. Conceptual strategies for
            routing service and required system upgrades will be discussed. Potential phasing of improvements will be
            discussed and uses that would necessitate facility upgrades will be evaluated. Building sizes and uses will be
            required to finalize system impacts and requirements, but conceptual level discussions will be based on the
            adopted Master Plan. The Consultant will also explore the possibility and location of joint utility trenches to
            facilitate service for multiple franchise utilities into the Heights District. Meetings will also discuss
            opportunities to extend new utility service into the Heights District while keeping service to the existing
            buildings and strategies for retrofitting utility service as proposed blocks redevelop.

            Northwest Natural
            Consultant will meet with Northwest Natural to review gas service capacity for the redeveloped Heights
            District, potential demand, and required infrastructure improvements. Potential phasing of improvements will
            be discussed and uses that would necessitate facility upgrades will be evaluated. Building sizes and uses will

            project area near the intersection between Devine Road and Mill Plain Boulevard.

                            Geotechnical Engineering
            Subtask 4.6.1: Geotechnical Site Evaluations
            Current project plans include infrastructure design to support the future buildout of multiple City blocks.
            Development will include improvements to existing City streets as well as construction of new streets. Future
            buildout will require disposal of stormwater collected on City streets and will likely be accomplished using
            roadside swales, trenches, and drywells. PBS’ current plans are to complete borings throughout the proposed
            development area to facilitate infiltration testing at depths of 5 and 20 feet below the existing ground surface
            (bgs), perform laboratory testing for correlation to hydraulic conductivity, and measure the depth to
            groundwater (if present within 30 feet of the ground surface). PBS will provide input regarding appropriate
            standard pavement sections based on soil type and consistency/relative density.

            Subtask 4.6.2: Geologic Map Review
            Geologic maps of the site area will be reviewed for information regarding geologic conditions at or near the
            site.

            Subtask 4.6.3: Subsurface Exploration
            Subsurface conditions will be explored by completing eighteen (18) borings using a truck-mounted drill rig.
            Borings will be advanced to depths of 30 feet bgs or practical refusal of the drilling equipment, whichever
            occurs first. In situ, standard penetration tests will be performed at 2.5- to 5-foot intervals. The borings will be
            logged, observed groundwater levels noted, and representative soil samples collected by a member of the
            PBS geotechnical engineering staff. Cuttings will be drummed and disposed of offsite.

            Subtask 4.6.4: Piezometer Installation
            Seven (7), 2-inch diameter PVC piezometer casings with 10 feet of screen will be installed at the site, one in
            each of two borings, to collect groundwater data during the required monitoring period. The piezometers will
            be equipped with a locking cap and protected with a flush, traffic-rated aluminum well monument. Data will
            be collected daily using pressure transducers and data loggers and will be downloaded twice during the
            monitoring period.

            Subtask 4.6.5: Field Infiltration Testing
            Eighteen (18) cased-hole, falling-head infiltration tests will be completed, one in each boring, at depths of 5 or
            20 feet bgs in general accordance with City of Vancouver test procedures. A soil sample will be collected
            immediately below the infiltration test depth for laboratory testing. Borings will be extended up to 10 feet
            below the infiltration test depth.

            Subtask 4.6.6: Soils Testing
            Samples will be returned to our laboratory and classified by the Unified Soil Classification System (ASTM
            D2487) and/or the Visual-Manual Procedure (ASTM D2488). Laboratory tests may include natural moisture
            contents, Atterberg limits, and grain-size analyses, as appropriate.

                            Traffic Engineering
            A traffic impact analysis (TIA) memorandum, dated August 30, 2019 by HDR, was prepared for The Heights
            District redevelopment plan. It addresses redevelopment within Zones 1, 2 and 3 in the vicinity of the Tower
            Mall area, which are planned to include 1,340 residential units and 204,000 square feet of commercial space as
            replacement for the existing under-utilized 258,000 square feet of commercial space. The TIA assumed no new
            commercial trips. Between the bus rapid transit (BRT) system currently being built on Mill Plain Boulevard and
            the planned multi-modal transportation improvements within the district, the TIA assumes a 6% reduction in
            trips. The original TIA assumed all new trips to be related to the proposed residential land use. During the AM
            peak hour 400 net new trips are estimated, with 100 entering and 300 exiting. During the PM peak hour 600
            net new trips are estimated, with 370 entering and 230 exiting.

            At the November 30, 2021, meeting, the City expanded the scope of work to include updating the TIA to
            address the replacement of the commercial land uses to the many years of vacant space at the Town Mall.

                     coordination, and lighting photometrics
                •    Draft and Final Access Management Plan (AMP) as appendix to traffic report


            Task 5: Permitting
            The project area is known not to contain critical areas or other regulated sensitive areas. The completion of
            critical area assessments or permitting outside of that typically required for civil infrastructure projects will not
            be necessary. As the initial master plans for the project were reviewed under the SEPA EIS process, the project
            will not require further review under SEPA unless there has been a significant change in the plans compared to
            what was initially reviewed.

            When federal monies are made available then the project will be required to comply with the National
            Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Based on the proposed project timeline, the NEPA review process can be
            initiated during further refinement beyond 30% without impacting delivery and construction timeframes.

                            Preliminary Permitting Assessment
            This task will include a review of the 30% design documents and the master plan SEPA EIS documentation to
            determine if additional SEPA review will be necessary in the future. This will culminate in the completion of a
            permitting matrix that will outline the steps, deliverables, and time frames necessary to achieve full project
            approval once federal funding is secured for the project and National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
            compliance is required. This matrix will serve as a roadmap for future project funding, planning, and
            scheduling efforts.

            Assumptions:
                1.   Federal funding will be used to fund the improvements
                2.   The project footprint will not significantly differ from what is contained within the EIS
                3.   The NEPA process will be completed through FHWA

            Deliverables:
                1.   Memo detailing SWPA review analysis
                2.   Permitting Matrix and Schedule

                            Permitting Preparation (Reserved)


            Task 6: 90% and Final Construction Documentation (Reserved)

            Dear Will,

            We appreciate the opportunity to submit the following proposal for providing landscape architectural
            services for The Heights District.

            Project Understanding and Team Roles:
                    1. The project includes master planning support, engagement support, and design
                       documentation to 30% level for parks, streets, and public use areas associated with the
                       redevelopment of the former Tower Mall site and surrounding district:
                         a. Parks include Civic Plaza, Neighborhood Park, and Cemetery Trail Connection
                         b. Landscape design for streets and public use areas
                    2. Walker Macy proposes the following sub-consultant team to assist us on the project and will
                       be contracted directly to Walker Macy:
                         • Fountain Designer: STO Design
                         • Irrigation Consultant: Land Arc Associates
                    3. Walker Macy's role will be to provide the following:
                         • For the Parks, Walker Macy, in collaboration with the design team, will document surface
                           improvements including paving (pedestrian), planting, grading, irrigation strategy, water
                           feature(s), site lighting layout, and site furnishings for areas within our scope.
                         • For the streets and public use areas, Walker Macy, in collaboration with the design team,
                           will document surface improvements including specialty paving finishes, planting, irrigation
                           strategy, site lighting layout, and site furnishings for areas within our scope.
                                o   FFF and/or PBS will provide street and public use area plans with proposed
                                    locations of curbs, sidewalks, and utilities for use as backgrounds in landscape
                                    drawings
                    4. The team’s civil engineer will be responsible for the following:
                         • Document all subsurface utilities, roadway, vehicular improvements, and any work within
                           the public right-of-way. We will collaborate with the civil engineer for road, parking, and site
                           design, as well as storm water quality features that may be included in our scope. Walker




                                                                                                                      Page 361 of 578
DocuSign Envelope ID: E7057AB0-19BC-4015-90C7-B1BF7710EEEF

            The Heights District
            January 21, 2022
            Page 2 of 6


                             Macy will lead documentation of grading for Parks and Civil Engineer will lead
                             documentation of grading for streets and public areas other than parks
                         • All erosion and sedimentation control documentation.
                    5. The team’s structural engineer will document structural information for all walls greater than
                       3’ in height and will document reinforcing for light pole foundations. The structural engineer
                       will be available to review structural components of Walker Macy details and will provide
                       signed and stamped structural calculations and redlines for details including but not limited to:
                       custom guardrails and handrails, custom bench supports, joist and structural support member
                       spacing and sizing for decks, fencing systems and structural footings, anchors and supports
                       for other elements.
                    6. The team's electrical engineer will document all lighting and electrical services. Walker Macy
                       will work with the team to select site fixtures and will include light fixtures in the landscape
                       layout plan. The electrical engineer will provide CAD files of the electrical fixture locations to
                       Walker Macy.
                    7. The team's cost estimating consultant will provide statements of probable costs. We will
                       review and evaluate cost estimates prepared by others for work within our scope.
                    8. City of Vancouver will be responsible for providing the following:
                         • A detailed site survey in AutoCAD 2013 or earlier format, suitable for construction
                           documentation, will be available for our use.
                         • Geotechnical Report of the project site.
                         • Arborist Report for the project site.

                                                               ATTACHMENT B
                                            DESCRIPTION OF SUBCONSULTANT’S SERVICES


            The Heights District Project
            Professional services for the Heights District Project will include update of the masterplan (Tower Mall
            Redevelopment Area), evaluation of site development configuration options, traffic engineering,
            evaluation of roundabouts and traffic signals, lighting designs, park design, landscape designs, structural
            designs, environmental process and permits, and utilities coordination and design. Coordination of
            services and deliverables will integrate with and support the Equitable Development Plan project’s
            recommended strategies and tools for culturally relevant and inclusive programming within the District
            and funding strategies to support one-time infrastructure and ongoing programmatic investments
            required to ensure equitable development of the Heights over the long-term. Additionally, project
            coordination and required federal documentation will be performed.
            The Project team includes:
                •     First Forty Feet – Overall Project Management, Master Planning, Urban Design, Strategic Planning,
                      Placemaking Strategies, Complete Street Design, and Community Engagement and
                      Communications support.
                •     PBS Engineering and Environmental Inc. – Civil Design, Permitting, Grant Funding Opportunities,
                      Communications Plan, Community Engagement and Communications support and summary
                      reporting.
                •     Walker Macy – Landscape architecture, Public Open Space Design, Park Design, and Lighting
                      Design Oversight
                •     Archaeological Investigations Northwest (AINW) – Cultural Resources Analysis
                •     DCW – Cost Management and Cost Estimating
                •     Leland Consulting Group – Capital Investment Strategy, and Real Estate Development Strategy


            Walker Macy (WM) will lead design programming, use programming and maintenance, design
            development, for the Civic Park (Plaza), and Neighborhood Park and prepare streets/public areas
            landscape design details, and plans to 30% Design Documentation. The firm will provide FFF Team
            support for project management meetings, review/work sessions, stakeholder engagement and
            preliminary/preferred concept analyses.

            Project Scope of Work
            The First Forty Feet Team will work with the City of Vancouver to provide public outreach and prepare the
            final master plan, construction drawings, specifications, cost estimates, permit documents and provide
            bidding and construction support.

            The Heights Project will complete master planning, construction, and permitting documents, for the
            development of public infrastructure including roadways, utilities, public spaces, wayfinding, and transit
            amenities within the 63-acre TMRA (Tower Mall Redevelopment Area).

            The following scope of work tasks describes how the Consultant Team will collaborate with Vancouver
            Parks, Recreation and Cultural Services Department (Parks), city staff, key stakeholders, community
            members, and regulatory agencies to prepare the final masterplan, construction drawings, specifications,
            cost estimates, permit documents, and provide bidding and construction support for the Heights Project’s
            public infrastructure.



            I. Project Scope of Work Tasks
    1.      Heights Project Orientation
            The First Forty Feet Team will coordinate with the City of Vancouver (COV) the Heights Project’s
            management structure, work plan, schedule, and coordination roles.

            Subtask 1.1 Contract Administration, Invoicing, and Progress Reports
            First Forty Feet will provide contract administration, invoicing, and progress reporting for the Project to
            the COV project manager including the following:
                1.   Prepare and submit monthly invoices. Each invoice will include date period covered by invoice,
                     number of hours worked during the billing period with billing rates shown; expenses; total cost
                     for labor and expenses for the billing period; subconsultants fees for the billing period; and a total
                     amount summarizing labor, expenses, and subconsultant fees.
                2.   Prepare a Contract Summary Report (CSR) to accompany the monthly invoices. The Contract
                     Summary Report will list each invoice as well as current invoice with an itemized summary of
                     invoice numbers, dates, and amounts billed for labor, expenses, and subconsultants as well as
                     total amounts for each invoice. The Contract Summary Report will also list the total amount billed
                     to date, total amount remaining under contract, and contract expiration date.
                3.   Maintain required contract documentation. Provide copies of project files and records to the city
                     for audits and public information requests. Final documents shall be provided in electronic format
                     as requested.


            WM Deliverable
            WM will provide the firm’s monthly invoicing and progress reporting to the FFF project manager no later
            than the fifth day of each month.

            Subtask 2.4 Project Engagement Milestones and Topics
            Engagement milestones will be the opportunities for engagement to identify a range of stakeholder
            perspectives to inform the Project’s preliminary and preferred concepts., public arts, gateways and
            wayfinding plan, interim and long-term public use area programming and on-site demonstration projects.
            Stakeholders will be given the opportunity to provide input so that the design of public infrastructure
            provides the most benefit to the communities it will serve.
            FFF and PBS will coordinate with the COV engagement with stakeholders at two Project milestones.
                •   Engagement Milestone #1 – Preliminary Concept Plans
                •   Engagement Milestone #2 – Preferred Concept Plan

            The FFF Team proposes two (2) engagement milestones with the Project stakeholders. Engagement
            Milestone #1 is intended to gather insights on preliminary public area (streets, plazas and parks) design
            concepts and alternatives; and Engagement Milestone #2 would review and provide feedback on the
            preferred public area (streets, plazas and parks) design concepts and alternatives. Engagement sessions
            will include one-on-one or group interviews, meetings, and feedback gathering through on-line surveys
            to be finalized in the Project’s Communications Plan.

            Task 3: Master Plan
            The FFF Team will build from the Heights District Plan’s development and programmatic elements
            supporting the internal and external street network and collection of public use areas through an iterative
            process of preliminary concepts development, identification of necessary refinements and concepts
            review to create a preferred concept for the Heights District’s network of street and public uses areas. The
            product of Task 3 will be 1). A comprehensive Field Guide, establishing the base condition with technical
            analyses of the Adopted Heights District Plan and supporting polices and regulations and 2). A Place
            Guide including a preferred concept, supporting cost estimating, phasing, and supporting plans and
            strategies that establishes the framework for Task 4 Design Development Documentation and preparation
            of the 30% Design submittal.

            Subtask 3.1 Field Guide
            The First Forty Feet Consultant team will obtain, assess, and review Project area background information
            and drawings including, but not limited to the Heights District Plan, Heights District Plan Appendices,
            Heights Final Planned Action Environmental Impact Statement, Draft Heights Plan District (HX Zone)
            regulations, Heights District Draft Urban Design Guidelines and other plans, standards, guidelines or
            documents identified and deemed necessary by the COV.

            First Forty Feet team will create a Field Guide document consisting of a preliminary site plan drawing, and
            summary report of the Project limits (Appendix A) design criteria (guidelines and standards) and
            programming for public use areas, streets and rights of way. The Field Guide enables the Project Team to
            confirm the design intentions of the Heights District Plan, assess and evaluate existing conditions,
            including planned and in-process infrastructure improvements and identify areas for possible plan
            adjustments, modifications or deviations. The Field Guide will establish the base condition for developing
            preliminary concepts and alternatives and a preferred concept plan that will be taken to 30% Design. The
            Field Guide will consist of the following elements:

            Subtask 3.1.1 Project Guidelines, Standards, and Program Elements
            The FFF Team will prepare a summary of the Heights Districts design guidelines, standards, and program
            elements for the Project area in excel spreadsheet and/or plan diagram exhibits for COV staff concurrence.
            Guidelines, standards and program elements will include but not be limited to:
                •   Heights District streets: including rights-of-way, typical street sections, and plans for E. Mill Plain
                    Boulevard, MacArthur Boulevard, N. Devine Road (Mill Plain Boulevard to MacArthur Boulevard, N.
                    Devine Road (Southeast Idaho Avenue to East 18th Street), N. Andresen Road, and the East
                    McLoughlin Area Safety Improvement Project
                •   Tower Mall Redevelopment Area internal streets: adopted Plan rights-of-way and typical street
                    sections consisting of the Loop Street (retail, residential, and festival street segments), Standard
                    Street, and Internal Street
                •   Planned round-a-bouts: including conceptual drawing plans and sections for RAB’s at N Devine
                    Road and N Andresen Road
                •   Planned BRT Stations: as-built drawing plans and sections for stations at E. Mill Plain Boulevard
                    and N. Devine Road and at E. Mill Plain Boulevard and N. Andresen Road.
                •   Public realm and open space: guidelines for the area (AC), location, program elements, and use
                    activities




                                                                                                                      Page 373 of 578
DocuSign Envelope ID: E7057AB0-19BC-4015-90C7-B1BF7710EEEF
                      34BB4AFD-D18D-472C-A071-8BB306806CC9




                •   Public Art and Wayfinding: guidelines for art and signage location, art features (representing
                    culture, history and environment), art typologies, signage type and standards; and gateway
                    elements (natural v. built)
                •   Gateways: guidelines for the Mill Plain and MacArthur intersection,
                •   Stormwater BMPs: guidelines for bio retention, overflow, and silva cell facilities for Loop retail,
                    Loop residential, and internal street typologies
                •   Landscaping: Tree CAP Standards, HX zone landscape standards, and native/adaptive plant
                    species list
                •   Urban forestry BMP: guidelines for soil volume amendments/silva cell details

            Roadways and utilities will include but not be limited to:
                •   Right-of-way
                •   Lane widths
                •   Curb return radii
                •   Sidewalks and curbs
                •   Curb extensions
                •   Universally accessible curb ramps
                •   Roadway cross-section
                •   Roadway section depth
                •   Design speed
                •   Design vehicle
                •   Transition tapers
                •   Max. and min. profile grades
                •   Vertical curve criteria
                •   Water/Sewer Mains
                •   Planting Types

            WM Deliverable
                •   Assemble and summarize guidelines, standards, and program elements for the public use areas,
                    including Civic Plaza, Neighborhood Park, Grand Loop, pocket parks and landscape standards for
                    streets.
                •   Attend up to two internal team meetings.


            Subtask 3.1.3: Adopted Heights District Plan: Preferred Concept Plan Assessment and Evaluation
            FFF will prepare an assessment and evaluation of the retail components of the activity center, civic
            park/plaza, neighborhood park and internal street alignments based on the criteria and fundamental
            characteristics for supporting retail, active public use areas and maximizing development potential within
            the Tower Mall Redevelopment Area. FFF criteria and fundamental characteristics will consider:
                •   Edge-to-edge retail configuration on both sides of the retail street
                •   Adequate drive-by traffic (5,000-15,000 ADT), visibility, and direct retail access
                •   Retail street design with on-street parking, bicycle access and parking, wide sidewalks to support
                    through pedestrian movement, retail display, outdoor seating and furnishings.
                •   Plaza activated on all sides, highly visible and directly accessible from surrounding streets

            Project Description:
            We understand that the project comprises cost planning for The Heights District Tower Mall
            Redevelopment Area Public Infrastructure Master Plan located in Vancouver, WA. The cost study scope
            of work includes costing the Masterplan and 30% Design documents.
            The adopted Heights District Plan is a community vision for how the Heights District will develop over the
            next 20 years. The district includes a variety of public open spaces, diverse mixed-income, mixed-use
            housing typologies, affordable to a wide range of community members, safe multi-modal mobility
            opportunities and access to transit. Standing at 63-acres, the Tower Mall Redevelopment Area (TMRA) is
            the focus of most of the redevelopment proposed in the Plan. The Grand Loop concept forms the basis of
            the Heights District Plan with the goal of the project being the completion of documents for the
            development of public infrastructure including roadways, utilities, public spaces, wayfinding, and transit
            amenities within the selected area.

                                        Staff Report: 173-26

To:       Mayor and City Council
From:     City Manager
Date:     September 14, 2026

Subject
Contract - First Amendment for Bridge Shelter Operations to Do Good Multnomah - C-101771

Key Points

    • The City previously contracted with Do Good Multnomah for Phase 1 of the Bridge Shelter
      project, which included operator participation in facility design and development of the shelter’s
      operational and program model. The proposed amendment adds Phase 2, operation of the
      completed facility.
    • The Bridge Shelter will provide 120 beds with 24/7 operations and onsite services intended to
      support stabilization and movement toward appropriate longer-term housing and treatment
      options.
    • The Phase 2 scope includes shelter staffing and operations, participant intake and case
      management, coordination with behavioral health, treatment and other system partners,
      kitchen and food-service operations, neighborhood impact management, data reporting, and
      ongoing evaluation and improvement.
    • The agreement will be placed on the same five-year contract cycle as the City’s four Safe Stay
      operating agreements, allowing the City to manage and evaluate its primary shelter contracts
      on a common schedule. Routine annual budget adjustments will be limited to applicable
      Consumer Price Index (CPI) increases.


Strategic Plan Alignment
Housing and Human Needs – meeting basic needs and partnering with organizations to support the
community

Safe and Prepared Community – a safe place to live, work, learn and play

Climate and Natural Systems – environmental stewardship and efforts to address climate change to
ensure a sustainable future

Economic Opportunity – a place where a wide variety of businesses of all sizes grow and thrive

Present Situation
The City is completing development of the Bridge Shelter, a 120-bed congregate shelter intended to
significantly expand Vancouver’s capacity to provide an alternative to unsheltered homelessness and
connect participants with behavioral health treatment, healthcare, housing, and other stabilization
services.

The City previously selected Do Good Multnomah as the Bridge Shelter’s primary service provider
and entered into a professional services agreement for Phase 1 of the project. During Phase 1, Do
Good worked with the City and project partners on facility design, operational planning, and

                                                                                            Page 389 of 578
development of the programming model. The proposed amendment moves the agreement into Phase
2 and establishes the scope and funding necessary for Do Good to operate the facility.

The Phase 2 scope requires 24/7 staffing and supervisory oversight appropriate for a shelter serving
individuals with complex needs. The Bridge Shelter will largely operate as a stabilization and triage-
focused interim shelter serving unsheltered adults and adult couples. The operator of this facility will
receive referrals through coordinated sources that include HART and City encampment-resolution
efforts, law enforcement and jail reentry coordination, hospitals and treatment facilities, behavioral
health providers, and other City-approved partners.

The program is intended to:

        • Provide immediate safety and basic needs stabilization;
        • Conduct and/or facilitate assessment of participant needs, including behavioral health,
          physical health, housing barriers, and system involvement;
        • Coordinate appropriate next-step placements based on realistic and sustainable outcomes;
        • Function as an integrated component of the City’s broader shelter, outreach, and
          homelessness response system.


Participants will have access to intake, case management, peer support, housing and systems
navigation, benefits assistance, care coordination, and employment and income stabilization support.
The scope specifically emphasizes ongoing participant engagement and individualized progress
toward stability rather than relying solely on rapid housing exits as the measure of success.
Sustainable outcomes may include permanent housing, supportive housing programs, Safe Stay or
other interim housing, detox or treatment programs, medical or long-term care placement, family
reunification, or other stable destinations consistent with participant goals and needs.

The shelter is also intended to function as part of the broader homelessness and behavioral-health
response system rather than as a stand-alone facility. The agreement requires coordination with the
City’s Safe Stay and Safe Park operators, HART, the onsite opioid treatment provider, Clark County
Jail and reentry programs, hospitals and treatment facilities, domestic violence providers, animal-
welfare partners, and the Council for the Homeless.

Do Good will manage the Bridge Shelter’s commercial kitchen and food-service program. Beyond
providing meals, the kitchen is intended to support participant health, and eventually, skill-building
and community engagement, including opportunities for job training and workforce development.

Similarly to the City’s existing Safe Stay Communities, the agreement also establishes specific
expectations for managing neighborhood impacts. Do Good will monitor the shelter perimeter and
immediately adjacent areas, address conditions reasonably associated with shelter operations,
reinforce participant expectations regarding surrounding public and private spaces, maintain
accessible communication with neighbors, and coordinate with the City when concerns arise.

Staff proposes placing this agreement on the same five-year contract cycle as the four Safe Stay
operating agreements being considered at a future Council meeting. Doing so will allow the City to
review its primary shelter operating contracts together, compare costs and performance across
programs, and reduce the administrative burden associated with maintaining multiple contract cycles
throughout the year. Routine annual budget adjustments will be limited to applicable CPI increases.
Because the Bridge Shelter is a new and significantly larger program, the agreement includes more
frequent review during its initial implementation. While the operator will submit monthly data reports,
this agreement also provides for quarterly contract review during the first year, twice-yearly review

                                                                                              Page 390 of 578
during the second year, and annual review beginning in year three, allowing the City and operator to
adjust operational practices as conditions and program needs evolve.

Advantage(s)

    1. Provides the operating agreement necessary to transition the Bridge Shelter from planning and
       development into active shelter operations.
    2. Maintains continuity between facility/program design and implementation by retaining Do Good
       Multnomah as the primary service provider for Phase 2.
    3. Establishes clear expectations for 24/7 shelter operations, participant services, system
       coordination, neighborhood impact management, reporting, and continuous program
       evaluation.
    4. Aligns the Bridge Shelter agreement with the City’s four Safe Stay operating agreements on a
       common five-year cycle, improving administrative efficiency and allowing more consistent
       evaluation of costs and performance across the City’s shelter system.


Challenge(s)

    1. The Bridge Shelter represents a significant expansion of the City’s shelter system and will
       serve a larger population with potentially higher and more complex service needs than the
       City’s existing Safe Stay Communities. Successful implementation will require ongoing
       coordination among Do Good, the City, healthcare providers, law enforcement and jail reentry
       partners, and other community partners and systems.
    2. As a new facility and service model for the City, actual operating needs and participant
       characteristics may differ from initial projections. The agreement’s enhanced review schedule
       and continuous improvement provisions are intended to allow the City and provider to identify
       and address operational issues as the program develops.


Budget Impact
This amendment increases the authorized amount of the professional services agreement by
$3,588,391.51, for a total agreement amount not to exceed $3,738,391.51. Future annual operating
budget adjustments during the five-year contract cycle will be limited to applicable CPI increases in
accordance with the agreement and subject to available appropriations.

Prior Council Review

    • November 6, 2023 - Council Meeting
    • December 9, 2024 - 2024 Homelessness Response Update
    • January 26, 2026 - 2025 Homelessness Response Update
    • Monthly Situation Reports


Action Requested
On Monday, September 14, 2026, authorize the City Manager, or designee, to finalize and execute
an amendment to the professional services agreement between the City of Vancouver and Do Good
Multnomah for Phase 2 operation of the Bridge Shelter.

                                                             Attachment A
                                                             Scope of Work



            The Contractor shall provide services to establish and operate an approximately 150-bed bridge shelter.
            This project will be executed in two phases:

                Phase 1: Consulting on Shelter Setup and Initial Operations
                Phase 2: Ongoing Operations and Continuous Improvement – to be awarded by amendment at a later
                date.

            Phase 1: Consulting on Shelter Setup and Initial Operations
            The Contractor will collaborate with the City and community stakeholders to develop and implement a
            comprehensive plan for the bridge shelter. Responsibilities include:

                    Facility Design, Layout and Preparation: Assist in the development of a trauma-informed,
                     welcoming environment that promotes safety, community-building, and well-being. The design
                     must integrate features that reduce isolation and foster meaningful connections among residents.
                     o Provide expertise on optimal site design and layout to maximize safety, accessibility, and
                         trauma-informed functionality.
                     o Assist with the coordination of the purchase of equipment/supplies necessary for eventual
                         operation of the bridge shelter.
                     o In partnership with the City, ensure the shelter facility is ready for occupancy, including
                         necessary renovations and safety inspections.

                    Program Development:
                     o Advise on the integration of evidence-based best practices and innovative approaches in shelter
                        operations, focusing on reducing barriers to stability, health, and permanent housing acquisition
                        and retention.
                     o Develop and finalize shelter policies, procedures, and program offerings that emphasize safety,
                        resiliency, appropriate personal accountability, and holistic support.
                     o Collaborate with people with current and/or former lived experience with homelessness, shelter
                        guests, and other relevant stakeholders to develop a culturally relevant and trauma-informed
                        base code of conduct.
                              Ensure that the base code of conduct addresses the specific needs and concerns of
                                 shelter participants.
                              Incorporate input and feedback from the community and the City of Vancouver to align
                                 the base code of conduct with their expectations for the bridge shelter.
                              Identify the process for exiting individuals not adhering to established Code of
                                 Conduct/Community Agreements.
                     o Establish case management/service delivery model focused on identifying and reducing barriers
                        to stability, housing, and overall well-being.




                                                                                                                   Page 402 of 578
Docusign Envelope ID: 3823CD9C-E6FB-43FD-8E85-11326B55CEE5




                     o   Establish process for coordination with co-located services, including the medication-assisted
                         treatment program and ongoing recovery supports.
                     o   Work with City staff, HART, relevant law enforcement and partner providers to establish
                         accessible, clear, and consistent referral and ongoing wraparound support coordination
                         processes for prospective shelter participants.
                     o   Establish partnerships and coordination process with external relevant service providers for
                         wrap-around support services.

               Staffing and Training:
                    o Recruit and train qualified staff reflective of the community to be served in the bridge shelter,
                        including individuals with lived experience of homelessness, addiction, and/or mental health
                        challenges.
                    o Provide comprehensive training on trauma-informed care, harm reduction, and other relevant
                        evidence-based practices.

               Community and Stakeholder Engagement
                   o Assist in identifying and establishing partnerships with other relevant service providers,
                     organizations, and stakeholders to promote culturally relevant, inclusive, and comprehensive
                     supportive service delivery.
                   o Support the City in designing a community engagement strategy, and participate in community
                     engagement activities, intended to build understanding and support for the bridge shelter.
                   o Engage with community stakeholders, service providers, and potential shelter residents to
                     gather input and feedback on Code of Conduct, service delivery model, and other shelter
                     needs/best practices.
                   o Engage with the bridge shelter’s surrounding community/neighborhood(s) to foster positive
                     relationships and develop a plan for mitigating any potential negative impacts.

               Performance Measures
                    o Collaborate with City to develop realistic benchmarks for success and identify additional key
                       performance indicators that align with the City’s core values and desired outcomes.

            Phase 2: Ongoing Operations and Continuous Improvement
            The Contractor will build upon Phase 1 scope of work and be responsible for the day-to-day operations of
            the bridge shelter, ensuring a safe, supportive, and structured environment appropriate for the previously
            described target population(s). Responsibilities for Phase 2 will be defined in an amendment upon

                                          Scope of Work

Phase 2: Bridge Shelter Ongoing Operations and Continuous Improvement

1. Staffing and Training for Bridge Shelter Operations.

1.1 The Provider shall maintain 24/7 staffing coverage with supervisory oversight. The Bridge
    Shelter will serve individuals with high and complex needs. The Provider shall staff and train
    appropriately to manage anticipated shelter-level acuity.

1.2 Training. Contractor shall train staff in the following areas:
        a. Trauma-informed care;
        b. Motivational interviewing;
        c. Harm reduction;
        d. De-escalation;
        e. Overdose response and Naloxone administration;
        f. CPR and first aid;
        g. Domestic violence awareness;
        h. Bloodborne pathogens and OSHA requirements;
        i. HMIS and incident documentation;
        j. Should we also include “other trainings coordinated by City”? (Since we pay CRMH to
           provide trainings for our whole system)

1.3 Staff Minimum Abilities. Contractor staff must be able to:
        a. Ensure site safety;
        b. Provide for regular case management engagement;
        c. Conduct perimeter checks;
        d. Respond to crisis situations.

1.4 When Problems Arise If patterns emerge indicating needs beyond the operational scope of a
    congregate shelter or Contractor capacity, the Contractor shall notify the City and participate
    in system-level planning to address service/capacity gaps.

2. Referral Activities.

2.1 Referral Process. Contractor shall develop a referral process to ensure effective partnerships
   with community organizations. Contractor must receive written approval from City before
   sharing the referral process with community organizations as described in Section X below.

2.2 Referral Partnerships. After its referral process is in place, Contractor shall partner with the
    following organizations to accept referrals for bridge shelter. City may approve additional
    referral partners in its discretion. Contractor shall partner with any City-approved referral
    partner. City may require Contractor to prioritize certain referrals based on City needs. :

Amendment No. 1                                                                    Page 4 of 14


                                                                                               Page 408 of 578
        a.   HART and City encampment resolution efforts;
        b.   Law enforcement and jail reentry coordination;
        c.   Local hospitals and treatment facilities;
        d.   Behavioral health providers;
        e.   Other City approved referral partners.

2.3 Prohibited Activities. Contractor shall not establish bed set-asides or referral exclusivity
    arrangements without the City’s prior written approval.

2.4 Records. Contractor shall maintain records related to the referral process that identify
    referral source, participant characteristics, and referral/placement outcomes. Contractor
    will make changes to include additional data in referral records upon City’s request.

3. Participant Eligibility.

3.1 Eligibility Criteria. Contractor shall develop participant eligibility criteria and screening
    process criteria and provide to City for written approval before implementation. Contractor
    shall submit any changes to these criteria for City’s written approval. For the avoidance of
    doubt, Contractor shall not create any eligibility criteria that would have the effect of:
    automatically disqualifying a participant for substance use, criminal history, system
    involvement, or high service needs unless the disqualification is required by law or necessary
    to mitigate imminent safety risk.

3.2 Eligibility of persons living unsheltered in Clark County. The City and County have agreed that
    the City will make available space to participants living unsheltered in Clark County for the
    first four years of this SOW. Contractor may not exclude participants based on their Clark
    County living status during this period.

3.3 HUD definitions exceptions. Contractor must implement certain exceptions related to persons
    covered under the HUD definition of literal homelessness (24 CFR 578.3), which City will
    provide in writing.

4. Participant Related Services.

4.1 Code of Conduct, Participant and Community Agreements and Behavioral Accountability
    Contractor shall develop a written code of conduct and participant and community
    agreements and provide to City for written approval prior to implementation.

4.1.1   Contractor’s Code of Conduct must:
        a. Promote safety and mutual respect;
        b. Outline expectations regarding cleanliness, shared spaces, and neighbor impact;
        c. Include graduated intervention steps prior to involuntary exit when feasible.
        d. Include process or description of opportunities for participants to provide input or
           feedback on code of conduct or agreements.
Amendment No. 1                                                                  Page 5 of 14


                                                                                             Page 409 of 578
4.2 Intake, Case Management, Stabilization (after eligibility determination)
    Contractor shall provide strengths-based, trauma-informed, and harm-reduction-oriented
    services to participants. Contractor’s services must include:
        a. Intake;
        b. Case management;
        c. Peer support;
        d. Housing and other systems’ navigation;
        e. Benefits enrollment support;
        f. Care coordination with treatment, healthcare, and other service providers;
        g. Employment and income stabilization support where appropriate.
        h. Other services as agreed by Parties.

4.3 Ongoing Participant Engagement. Contractor may use specific planning tools in connection
    with participants (e.g., WRAP, Independent Service Plans), however, Contractor must engage
    with participants as part of structured stabilization efforts at least weekly. Contractor shall
    promote appropriate next-step transitions to participants and ensure participants continue
    to progress in their individual stability, including through goal development and
    individualized support to modify and achieve those goals.

4.4 Participant Incidents. Contractor must document and report all incidents that require
    emergency services to City within 24 hours . However, incidents that involve serious physical
    harm or injury and other similar incidents must be reported within four hours. Contractor
    shall report to the City the person(s) involved, incident type, and outcome.

4.5 Participant Involuntary Exits. Contractor may remove participants immediately when
    participant behavior poses a threat to others’ safety as determined by Contractor.
    Contractor shall document and report involuntary exits to the City within one business day
    of the exit.

5. General Operations

5.1 Coordination with System Partners. Contractor shall operate the Bridge Shelter as part of a
    coordinated system, not as an isolated program. Contractor shall coordinate with:

       a.   City Safe Stay and Safe Park operators;
       b.   City Homeless Assistance and Resources Team (HART)
       c.   Northstar Clinic, the onsite Mobile Opioid Treatment services provider;
       d.   Clark County Jail/jail re-entry programs;
       e.   In-patient and outpatient facilities, including hospitals and treatment centers;
       f.   Domestic violence service providers;
       g.   The Southwest Washington Humane Society and other animal welfare partners;
       h.   Council for the Homeless and Homeless Management Information System (HMIS)
            administrators.

5.2 Severe Weather and Emergency Operations. Contractor shall develop a continuity-of-
    operations plan to ensure services remain available 24 hours per day, seven days a week in

5.2.1. Expanded Capacity during Severe Weather. Contractor may activate expanded capacity

prior to implementation. Activation criteria must align with the Clark County Severe Weather
Taskforce (facilitated by Council for the Homeless) criteria in effect at the time of the severe
weather event. Contractor shall inform City and the Clark County Severe Weather Taskforce of
plan activation as soon as the Contractor decides to activate the plan.

maintenance, janitorial, and upkeep of the Bridge Shelter, and may do so through in-house
services or by contract with a third-party contractor. Contractor will be in the best position to
timely notify the City of any maintenance or janitorial service needs at the Bridge Shelter. As
such, Contractor must notify the City of any maintenance or janitorial service needs that it
discovers at the Bridge Shelter within 24 hours of discovery by Contractor. Failure to timely notify
City may constitute a material breach of this Agreement. City will provide and train Contractor

                                        Staff Report: 174-26

To:       Mayor and City Council
From:     City Manager
Date:     September 14, 2026

Subject
Contract - Amendment to the Fire Department Services Agreement with Fire District No. 5

Key Points

    • On August 24, 2026, Fire Chief Drake presented a workshop to Council outlining how
      additional support staff, fully funded by Fire District 5, can help advance the department’s
      strategic plan goals.
    • To move forward with this proposal, staff have prepared an amendment to the services
      agreement with Fire District 5 which states the District will reimburse the City for 7.0 limited
      duration FTEs at 100% of actual costs through 2029. Costs are anticipated to be
      approximately $3 million.
    • In order to begin hiring the 7.0 limited duration FTEs in the 2025-2026 biennium, certain
      adjustments to the appropriation, FTE, and salary schedules are required by a separate
      Council budget ordinance. That ordinance is scheduled for its first reading tonight and second
      reading and public hearing on September 21, 2026.
    • The amendment also updates the parties' invoicing obligations under the agreement.


Strategic Plan Alignment
Safe and Prepared Community – a safe place to live, work, learn and play

Present Situation
The City of Vancouver and Clark County Fire District 5 (CCFD5) have maintained a cooperative fire
services agreement since 1994, which has periodically been updated by the parties. Under the terms
of the current agreement, CCFD5 funds a portion of the Vancouver Fire Department (VFD) operating
and capital costs.

In April 2026, Chief Drake presented a support staff funding proposal to the CCFD5 Board, which it
approved. Chief Drake provided an overview of this proposal to the Council at an August 24, 2026
workshop. The proposal tied progress on several VFD strategic plan outcomes to the addition of 7.0
support staff at VFD. The proposed positions are as follows:

    • 1.0 Administrative Assistant 3
    • 1.0 Data Analyst 1
    • 1.0 Fire Emergency Services Manager
    • 1.0 Fire Professional Standards Program Manager
    • 1.0 Material Control Coordinator
    • 2.0 Support Specialist 2


As part of this proposal, CCFD5 would fund 100% of actual position costs including ancillary

                                                                                            Page 419 of 578
expenses for these positions through December 2029. Actual costs for this period are expected to be
around $3,000,000.

In an effort to move forward with hiring these limited-duration positions in the 2025-2026 biennium,
staff have prepared a related supplemental budget ordinance for Council's consideration; the
ordinance's first reading is scheduling for tonight and its second reading and public hearing are
scheduled for September 21, 2026.

The amendment also updates the terms of general reimbursement invoicing from the City of
Vancouver to CCFD5. The City will invoice 22.8% (as adjusted from time to time pursuant to the
agreement) of actual costs incurred, on a quarterly basis.

Advantage(s)

    1. Approving this amendment will allow the Fire Department to move forward with hiring 7.0
       limited duration support staff contingent on City's Council determination on the separate
       budget ordinance. These support staff will help advance the Fire Department’s strategic plan,
       and support community safety.
    2. CCFD5 will reimburse 100% of the City's actual costs for these positions.


Challenge(s)
Clark County Fire District 5 has agreed to fund position costs through 2029. Therefore, these are
limited duration positions and there is no source of funds identified to retain these positions after
December 2029.

Budget Impact
The addition of 7.0 limited-duration positions is expected to generate approximately $3.0 million in
additional costs from the 4th quarter of 2026 through December 2029. Actual position costs including
associated ancillary costs will be 100% funded by Clark County Fire District 5. Position, salary
schedule, and budget appropriation impacts are addressed in the Supplemental Budget Adjustment
Related to Clark County Fire District No. 5 Amended Agreement ordinance, scheduled for first
reading tonight and second reading and public hearing on September 21, 2026.

Prior Council Review
Ctiy Council Workshop - August 24, 2026

Action Requested
On Monday, September 14, 2026, authorize the City Manager, or designee, to enter into amended
services agreement with Clark County Fire District 5 following the adoption of an implementing
budget ordinance.

Kathryn Shifley, Chief Financial Officer, John Drake, Fire Chief, katie.shifley@cityofvancouver.us,
John.Drake@cityofvancouver.us
