                                        Staff Report: 175-26

To:       Mayor and City Council
From:     City Manager
Date:     September 14, 2026

Subject
Acceptance of Grant from Ed and Dollie Lynch Fund Through Community Foundation for Southwest
Washington for Temporary County Homeless Assistance and Resource Team Outreach Expansion

Key Points

    • The City of Vancouver and Clark County are partnering to expand the Homeless Assistance
      and Resource Team (HART) model into areas of Clark County beyond Vancouver city limits,
      creating a more coordinated regional approach to unsheltered homelessness and supporting
      access to the City’s new bridge shelter.
    • Under the funding partnership for construction of the bridge shelter, individuals experiencing
      homelessness in Clark County, outside of Vancouver, will be eligible to access the facility for
      four years after opening. Expanded outreach capacity in the county will help identify, engage
      and facilitate referrals for individuals who may benefit from the new shelter capacity.
    • The $564,100 grant will fully fund up to four limited-term outreach positions, including capacity
      for coordination of the expanded outreach effort, as well as salaries and benefits, vehicles,
      technology, equipment and other associated costs; no local City match is required.
    • Clark County has separately approved funding for a dedicated Clark County Sheriff’s Office
      Deputy to support the expanded HART effort. Additional operational components and inter-
      agency coordination are still under development.


Strategic Plan Alignment
Housing and Human Needs – meeting basic needs and partnering with organizations to support the
community

Safe and Prepared Community – a safe place to live, work, learn and play

Climate and Natural Systems – environmental stewardship and efforts to address climate change to
ensure a sustainable future

High Performing Government – a government that is reliable, fiscally responsible, equitable, and
open to compromise

Present Situation
The City’s Homeless Assistance and Resources Team (HART) is a multidisciplinary team that
addresses the impacts of unsheltered homelessness through coordinated outreach, service
connection, encampment assessment and cleanup, and enforcement when necessary. HART brings
together staff from the City Manager’s Office, Vancouver Police Department and Public Works
Department to provide a coordinated response to unsheltered homelessness in public spaces. The
HART model is intended to balance two responsibilities that must occur together: helping individuals
experiencing homelessness access services, shelter and pathways toward greater stability, while also

                                                                                            Page 445 of 578
maintaining public spaces for their intended and shared community use. HART staff prioritize
engagement, problem-solving and voluntary connection to available resources. In cases where those
efforts are unsuccessful and public health, safety, environmental or access concerns remain, the
multidisciplinary structure allows the team to coordinate an appropriate response using the other tools
available to local government.

Both the City and Clark County have historically funded nonprofit outreach services for individuals
experiencing homelessness within their respective jurisdictions. As the City and County increasingly
share homelessness response resources and infrastructure, however, there is value in developing a
more coordinated governmental approach across jurisdictional boundaries. That need is particularly
important with the upcoming opening of the City’s 120-bed bridge shelter. Clark County contributed
funding toward construction of the facility, and as part of that partnership, individuals experiencing
homelessness in Clark County will be eligible for shelter placement for four years following opening.
Ensuring that this capacity can effectively serve residents of both jurisdictions requires outreach and
referral capacity in the areas from which shelter residents will be coming.

The City and County are working together to expand the HART model beyond Vancouver city limits,
beginning with additional outreach capacity that can operate throughout Clark County. The expansion
of HART into the County is intended to build upon the multidisciplinary approach developed through
the City’s existing HART program, combining outreach and engagement with coordinated
governmental response to unsheltered homelessness and its impacts on public spaces and Clark
County residents, both housed and unhoused.

Clark County has approved funding for a dedicated Clark County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO) Deputy to
support this effort. The City and County are continuing to develop the operational structure and
agreements necessary for implementation, including Public Works coordination and the respective
roles and responsibilities of participating departments and agencies. Because outreach and
engagement can begin independently, the City is moving forward with establishing that capacity while
the operational structure and necessary agreements continue to be developed.

The Ed and Dollie Lynch Fund, through the Community Foundation for Southwest Washington, has
offered the City a $564,100 grant to support the outreach portion of the work for an initial one-year
period. The grant will fully fund up to four limited-term outreach positions, including capacity for
coordination of the expanded outreach effort, as well as salaries and benefits, vehicles, technology,
equipment and other associated costs. Outreach staff will engage individuals living unsheltered in
other areas of Clark County, connect them with available services and supports, facilitate referrals to
the bridge shelter and other appropriate shelter or housing resources, and coordinate with Clark
County, CCSO, nonprofit outreach providers and other community partners and service providers.

The expansion also builds upon the City’s existing partnership with Clark County through Community
Court. Community Court provides an alternative response for eligible low-level offenses by combining
accountability with connections to services intended to address underlying barriers. Greater
coordination among HART outreach staff, law enforcement and other partners creates an opportunity
to more consistently connect eligible individuals in unincorporated Clark County with that existing
regional resource when appropriate. While Clark County has historically supported countywide
homelessness response efforts, the City has made significant additional investments in recent years
to address the disproportionate impacts of unsheltered homelessness within Vancouver. Those
investments have included dedicated City outreach and response through HART, expanded shelter
capacity, and other services and interventions designed specifically to address unsheltered
homelessness and its impacts.

The proposed HART expansion represents an opportunity to build upon both those City investments

                                                                                             Page 446 of 578
and the County’s existing regional system by extending a coordinated governmental response model
beyond Vancouver and better connecting that response with the services and resources already
shared across the community. People experiencing homelessness routinely move across
jurisdictional boundaries, and effective outreach and engagement do not always fit neatly within those
boundaries. Providing outreach staff the flexibility to maintain engagement with individuals as they
move throughout Clark County, while coordinating with the public agencies responsible for various
operational responses within each jurisdiction, will support continuity of engagement with individuals
experiencing unsheltered homelessness and greater consistency in homelessness response efforts
across local jurisdictions. It will also help make more effective use of shared investments, including
the bridge shelter and Community Court.

Advantage(s)

   1. Expands outreach and service engagement for individuals experiencing unsheltered
      homelessness in Clark County.
   2. Establishes referral capacity necessary to support Clark County residents’ access to the bridge
      shelter.
   3. Creates greater consistency and coordination between City and County homelessness
      response efforts.
   4. Builds upon existing City-County partnerships, including Community Court, and supports
      appropriate utilization of that resource.
   5. Leverages private philanthropic funding to establish regional outreach capacity without
      requiring a City local match.
   6. Supports more effective use of public investments in shelter and homelessness response by
      pairing additional shelter capacity with active outreach, engagement and referral.
   7. Supports more effective use of public investments in shelter and homelessness response by
      pairing additional shelter capacity with active outreach, engagement and referral.


Challenge(s)

   1. The expansion adds four limited-term positions and a new geographic service area to a City-
      managed program. The City and Clark County are continuing to develop the interagency
      agreements, roles, responsibilities and operational procedures necessary to support
      implementation of the full multidisciplinary HART model, to include County law enforcement
      and Public Works.
   2. The initial grant provides funding for one year. Continued operation beyond the grant period
      will depend upon evaluation of the expanded effort and identification of future funding.


Budget Impact
No anticipated budget impact.

Prior Council Review

    • November 6, 2023 – Council meeting
    • December 9, 2024 – Homeless Emergency Response Update workshop
    • December 16, 2024 – City Council Meeting
    • June 16, 2025 – Acceptance of prior grant supporting temporary HART outreach expansion
    • Monthly situation reports

      A RESOLUTION adopting amended Investment Policies for the City of Vancouver.

                                         Staff Report: 176-26

To:       Mayor and City Council
From:     City Manager
Date:     September 14, 2026

Subject
Resolution Adopting Updated City Investment Policy

Key Points

    • The City's investment policy, last adopted in 2012, is being modernized to reflect over a
      decade of evolution in financial markets, Washington State requirements, and public-sector
      standards.
    • The City's investment priorities will continue to be, in order of importance, safety of principal,
      maintaining sufficient liquidity, and achieving a reasonable rate of return consistent with those
      priorities.


Strategic Plan Alignment
High Performing Government – a government that is reliable, fiscally responsible, equitable, and
open to compromiseppets in editing menu for this section.

Present Situation
The City's current Investment Policy was adopted in 2012 and has provided a framework for
managing the City's investment portfolio for more than a decade. During that time, investment
markets, financial-management practices, Washington State requirements, and professional
standards applicable to public-sector investment programs have continued to evolve.


The City's investment philosophy has remained conservative and focused on protecting public funds.
The proposed update does not change that philosophy. The City's investment priorities will continue
to be, in order of importance, safety of principal, maintaining sufficient liquidity, and achieving a
reasonable rate of return consistent with those priorities.

The proposed policy update is intended to bring the City's written policy into better alignment with
current investment practices and recognized public-sector standards. It provides greater clarity
regarding the responsibilities of the City Council, City Manager, Investment Officer, and Finance staff
and establishes a more clearly defined framework for managing the City's investment program.

The update also addresses areas that have become increasingly important in public-sector
investment management, including diversification, credit quality, investment maturities, internal
controls, documentation, training, performance reporting, and procedures for securities that
experience a credit-rating downgrade.

The proposed policy updates the City's list of authorized investments to provide appropriate flexibility
within the investments permitted under Washington State law. At the same time, the policy

                                                                                              Page 451 of 578
establishes limits intended to manage credit risk, interest-rate risk, concentration risk, and liquidity
risk. Prohibited investments are also identified to provide clear direction to staff.

Another important component of the update is improved investment reporting. The revised policy
establishes clearer expectations for monitoring and reporting portfolio performance and provides for
the use of appropriate benchmarks, including the Washington State Local Government Investment
Pool when applicable. This will provide Council with more consistent information regarding the City's
investment portfolio and its performance.

Overall, the proposed update is primarily a policy modernization and governance effort. It is not
intended to change the City's level of investment risk or encourage staff to pursue higher returns at
the expense of safety or liquidity.


Advantage(s)

    1. Strengthens overshight, accountability, and internal controls.
    2. Improves flexibility and risk management within conservative investment limits.
    3. Enhances transparency through clearer reporting and performance management.


Challenge(s)
None

Budget Impact
None

Prior Council Review
Council workshop - August 24, 2026

Action Requested
On Monday, September 14, 2026, finalize and approve the resolution to update the City Investment
Policy.

  Title: Investment Policy


  Policy and Procedure Number:            Supersedes (Number and Title):


  Citywide policy

  Effective Date:                         Approved by (Name, Title and Signature):




Purpose: The purpose of this Policy is:

   •    To establish investment objectives and parameters necessary to safeguard public funds
        entrusted to the City of Vancouver (the City).

   •    To articulate the City Council’s intent for the governance over the City’s investments.

   •    To communicate clear policy and strategy guidelines for the City’s investment
        administration.

   •    To demonstrate a transparent and accountable stewardship plan to the community.


Policy Statement: It is the policy of the City to invest public funds in a manner that safeguards
and protects the principal of the City’s investments, provides liquidity in meeting daily cash flow,
and provides the highest return possible through budgetary and economic cycles. All investment
activity will be in compliance with chapter 35.39 RCW “Fiscal - Investment of funds,” chapter 39.59
RCW “Public Funds – Authorized investments,” and any other statutes or regulatory requirements,
such as Internal Revenue Codes, which may apply.

1.0 – Scope
This investment policy applies to all financial assets of the City of Vancouver. These funds are
accounted for in the City’s Annual Financial Report and include:
   1.   General Fund
   2.   Special Revenue Funds
   3.   Capital Projects Funds
   4.   Enterprise Funds
   5.   Trust and Agency Funds
   6.   Internal Services Funds
   7.   Public Facilities Funds
   8.   Debt Service Funds (Unless prohibited by Bond indentures)
   9.   Any new fund created by City ordinance, unless specifically exempted
Should bond covenants be more restrictive than this policy, funds shall be invested in full
compliance with those restrictions.

Investments of the City’s funds may be made on a pooled basis across all funds, with principal
and interest apportioned for the benefit of the various participating funds or for the benefit of the
General Fund. (RCW 35.39.034)


2.0 – Authority to Invest
Enabling Legislation

All investments shall be managed in a manner responsive to public trust, consistent with state
statutes (Revised Code of Washington (RCW)). Authority to manage the City’s investment
program is derived from RCW sections 35A.40.050, 35.39.032, 36.29.020 and from the applicable
sections of the City Code.

                                                                                                   2




                                                                                                Page 456 of 578
                                                                            CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                          Policies and Procedures



 Delegation of Authority

 The City Council, as the governing body, will retain ultimate fiduciary responsibility for the City’s
 investment portfolio. The City Council shall receive monthly investment reports, and review and
 adopt any changes to the investment policy.


 In accordance with City Charter Section 3.03, the City Manager, as head of the administrative
 branch of the city government, shall provide executive oversight of the City’s investment program
 and shall appoint the Finance Director (or his/her designee) to serve as the City’s Investment
 Officer. The Investment Officer is authorized to manage the City’s investment program and
 executive investment transactions in accordance with this Policy.


 No person may initiate investment transactions on behalf of the Investment Officer without the
 express written consent of the Investment Officer. The Finance Director shall be responsible for
 the administration and day-to-day operation of the investment program, including the
 development and implementation of investment strategies for all funds held by or belonging to
 the City.


 Training
 All staff engaging in investment transactions shall attend public investment training, which may
 include staff training by a qualified finance professional. Staff shall not engage in any allowable
 investment transaction for which they cannot articulate a rationale for having done so.


 Contracted Management

 The City may engage the services of an external investment advisor to assist in the management
 of the City’s investment portfolio in a manner consistent with the City’s objectives. Such external
 advisors may be granted non-discretionary authority to purchase and sell investment securities in
 accordance with this Investment Policy. Such advisors must be registered under the Investment
 Advisers Act of 1940. Any external investment manager engaged to assist in the management of
 the City’s investment portfolio will be held to the prudent investor standard of care (RCW
 11.100.020).


 3.0 – Objectives
1.     Safety. Safety of principal is the foremost objective of the City’s investment policy. City
       investments shall be made in a manner that seeks to ensure the preservation of capital in
       the overall portfolio. To mitigate credit and interest rate risk, investment decisions shall be

                                                                                                    3




                                                                                                 Page 457 of 578
                                                                               CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                             Policies and Procedures



      undertaken in a manner that seeks to ensure the preservation of capital in the overall
      portfolio.

     a.     Credit risk. This is the risk of loss due to the financial failure of the security issuer or
            backer. The City will minimize credit risk by:

           (1)    Limiting exposure to poor credits and concentrating the
                  investments in the safest types of securities;
           (2)    Diversifying the investment portfolio so that potential losses
                  on individual securities will be minimized; and
           (3)    Actively monitoring the investment portfolio holdings for
                  rating changes, changing economic market conditions, etc.

     b.     Interest rate risk. This is the risk that the market value of securities in the portfolio will
            fall due to increases in general interest rates. The City will mitigate interest rate risk
            by:

           (1)    Structuring the investment portfolio so that securities mature
                  to meet cash requirements, when known, for ongoing
                  operations, thereby avoiding the need to sell securities on the
                  open market prior to maturity;
           (2)    Investing liquidity funds primarily in short-term instruments
                  (i.e., investments maturing in less than one year); and
           (3)    Investing excess liquidity funds in a manner that is consistent
                  with the established risk/return objectives of this policy within
                  the stated maximum weighted average maturity constraint.


2.    Liquidity. The City's investment portfolio will remain sufficiently liquid to enable the City to
      meet all reasonably anticipated operating requirements. This will be accomplished by either
      maintaining a portion of the portfolio in investment vehicles offering daily liquidity at face
      value, such as the Washington State Local Government Investment Pool (LGIP), or
      structuring the portfolio so that securities mature concurrently with cash needs to meet
      anticipated demands. Because all possible cash demands cannot be anticipated, the
      portfolio should consist largely of securities with active secondary or resale markets.

3.    Return on investment. The City's investment portfolio shall be designed with the objective
      of attaining a market rate of return throughout budgetary and economic cycles, taking into
      account the City’s investment risk constraints, the cash flow characteristics of the portfolio,
      and earnings relative to the State of Washington LGIP. Return on investment is of lesser
      importance compared to the safety and liquidity objectives described above.


                                                                                                        4




                                                                                                     Page 458 of 578
                                                                          CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                        Policies and Procedures



4.0 – Prudence
The standard of prudence to be used by investment officials shall be the “prudent investor
standard,” which, as enacted by State Statute (RCW 11.100.020), says:
           (1)    A trustee shall invest and manage trust assets as a prudent
                  investor would, by considering the purposes, terms,
                  distribution requirements, and other circumstances of the
                  trust. In satisfying this standard, the trustee shall exercise
                  reasonable care, skill, and caution.
           (2)    A trustee's investment and management decisions respecting
                  individual assets must be evaluated not in isolation but in the
                  context of the trust portfolio as a whole and as a part of an
                  overall investment strategy having risk and return objectives
                  reasonably suited to the trust.


Investment officers acting in accordance with the written procedures and exercising due diligence
shall be relieved of personal responsibility for individual securities’ credit risk or marketplace
changes, provided deviations from expectations are reported in a timely fashion and appropriate
action is taken to control adverse developments.


5.0 – Ethics and Conflict of Interest
Officers and employees involved in the investment process shall refrain from, or disclose, personal
business activity that could conflict with proper execution of the investment program, or which
could impair their ability to make impartial investment decisions. Employees and officers shall
subordinate their personal interests to those of the City, particularly with regard to the time of
purchases and sales. However, an employee is unlikely to personally own a controlling interest in
a security that becomes the best investment for the City, such as a highly rated medium-term note
issuer, and should not have to sell their personal position in order to serve the City.


   •   Disclosure. Employees and investment officials shall disclose in writing to the City
       Manager any material financial interests in the financial institutions to conduct business
       within this jurisdiction, and they shall further disclose any large personal
       financial/investment positions that could be related to the performance of the portfolio.
       Employees and officers shall refrain from, or disclose, any personal investment transactions
       with the same agents with whom business is conducted on behalf of the City and shall
       avoid, or disclose, transactions that might impair public confidence.




                                                                                                 5




                                                                                              Page 459 of 578
                                                                             CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                           Policies and Procedures



   •   Gifts. Officers and employees involved in the investment process may not accept any
       valuable gift, favor or gratuity which is made on the basis of his or her position in the City’s
       service.


6.0 – Authorized Financial Dealers and Institutions
   •   Brokers. The Investment Officer or his/her designee will maintain a list of
       broker/dealers, which are authorized to provide investment services. To be eligible
       to do business with the City, a broker/dealer must provide a Broker/Dealer
       Questionnaire that includes the following: audited financial statements, current
       securities-related licensing; proof of registration and licenses held with the
       Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA); proof of registration with the
       State of Washington Securities Division; provide current active municipal client
       references; and certification of having read the City’s current investment policy.
       The financial condition of qualified brokers will be reviewed annually by the
       Investment Officer.

   •   Banks. Banking services, depository accounts and certificates of deposit, as required by
       state law, (RCW 39.58), may be contracted only with those institutions approved by the
       Washington Public Deposit Protection Commission (PDPC)


7.0 – Authorized Investments
Investment authority is governed by VMC 2.10.030, which authorizes the Finance Director to invest
City funds in accordance with state law. Pursuant to that authority and applicable provisions of
state law (including, without limitation, RCW 39.59.020, 39.59.030, 43.84.080, and 43.250.040,
including all future amendments) the City may invest in various securities, including, without
limitation, the following:

Local Government Investment Pool (LGIP)
The Washington State Local Government Investment Pool (LGIP) provides local governments
with a secure, highly liquid investment option for managing short-term funds. The LGIP is
administered by the Washington State Treasurer and invests in a diversified portfolio of high-
quality, short-term investments in accordance with state law and investment policies.

Clark County Investment Pool
The Clark County Investment Pool is a pooled investment program administered by the Clark
County Treasurer that allows local governments to combine funds for investment purposes.
Participation in the pool provides daily liquidity, professional portfolio management, and
diversification consistent with applicable state laws and investment policies.
                                                                                                     6




                                                                                                  Page 460 of 578
                                                                            CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                          Policies and Procedures




U.S. Treasury Obligations
Direct obligations of the United States Treasury with the full faith and credit of the United States.

U.S. Agency Obligations
U.S. Government Agency obligations and U.S. Government Sponsored Enterprises (GSEs),
including but not limited to Federal Farm Credit Banks Funding Corporation (FFCB), Federal
Home Loan Bank (FHLB), Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (FHLMC), and Federal
National Mortgage Association (FNMA).

Repurchase Agreements
Repurchase agreements for securities provided that the transaction is structured so that the City
obtains control over the underlying securities. If utilized, a Master Repurchase Agreement must
be executed by the Finance Director with the transacting bank or dealer. Collateral must meet
the authorized investment and maturity constraints of this policy.

Bankers’ Acceptances
Bankers’ acceptances purchased on the secondary market that, at the time of purchase, are
rated in the highest short-term rating category by at least two nationally recognized statistical
rating organizations (NRSROs), including A-1 by Standard & Poor’s, P-1 by Moody’s, F1+ by
Fitch, or equivalent ratings.

Commercial Paper
Commercial paper provided that the Finance Director adheres to the policies and procedures of
the State Investment Board regarding commercial paper (RCW 43.84.080(7)); the City will not
allow asset-backed commercial paper. Commercial paper shall not have maturities exceeding
270 days and must be purchased on the secondary market rather than directly from issuers.

Commercial paper must be rated at the time of purchase in the highest short-term rating
category by at least two NRSROs, including A-1 by Standard & Poor’s, P-1 by Moody’s, F1+ by
Fitch, or equivalent ratings. If rated by more than two NRSROs, the security must receive the
highest short-term rating from all rating agencies providing ratings.

Any commercial paper purchased with a maturity greater than 100 days must also have a long-
term senior unsecured debt rating of at least AA- by Standard & Poor’s or Fitch, Aa3 by
Moody’s, or equivalent ratings.

The City will utilize an Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) framework as part of its due
diligence process for corporate investments. The ESG methodology shall be developed by the
Finance Director using recognized industry standards and available third-party research and


                                                                                                    7




                                                                                                Page 461 of 578
                                                                           CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                         Policies and Procedures



shall be periodically reviewed and updated to ensure consistency, transparency, and alignment
with the City's investment objectives.

If a commercial paper holding is downgraded below these minimum standards after purchase,
the Finance Director shall review the holding and determine whether continued ownership is
prudent and consistent with the objectives of this Investment Policy.

Commercial paper and corporate notes combined shall not exceed 25 percent of the total
market value of the investment portfolio at the time of purchase.

Certificates of Deposit / Bank Deposits / Savings
Investment deposits including certificates of deposit with qualified public depositories as
defined by RCW 39.58.010(2) and in accordance with applicable statutory requirements.

If not 100 percent collateralized, the depository institution must be rated in the highest short-
term rating category by at least one NRSRO, including A-1 by Standard & Poor’s, P-1 by
Moody’s, F1+ by Fitch, or equivalent ratings.

Bonds of the State of Washington
Bonds of the State of Washington and any local government in the State of Washington rated
A- or better at the time of investment by a nationally recognized rating agency.

General Obligation Bonds of Other States or Local Governments
General obligation bonds of states other than Washington and their local governments rated A-
or better at the time of investment by a nationally recognized rating agency.

Corporate Notes
No corporate fixed-income issuer may exceed 3 percent of the total portfolio market value.

The maximum percentage of corporate notes that may be purchased from any single issuer
rated AA- or better by at least two NRSROs (or all available NRSROs if fewer than two exist) is 3
percent of the total portfolio market value.

The maximum percentage of corporate notes that may be purchased from any single issuer
rated A+, A, or A- by any major rating agency is 2 percent of the total portfolio market value.

The City will utilize an Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) framework as part of its due
diligence process for corporate investments. The ESG methodology shall be developed by the
Finance Director using recognized industry standards and available third-party research and
shall be periodically reviewed and updated to ensure consistency, transparency, and alignment
with the City's investment objectives.

                                                                                                    8




                                                                                               Page 462 of 578
                                                                              CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                            Policies and Procedures




Corporate notes must be purchased on the secondary market and not directly from the issuer.

If securities are downgraded below these minimum standards after purchase, they shall remain
eligible holdings and may be held or sold at the discretion of the Finance Director.

Commercial paper and corporate notes combined shall not exceed 25 percent of the total
market value of the investment portfolio at the time of purchase.

Supranational Bonds
Supranational bonds issued by international financial institutions established by agreements
among nations, with member nations contributing capital and participating in management. The
City may only purchase bonds issued by institutions for which the United States is the largest
shareholder.

Eligible supranational securities shall carry a long-term credit rating of at least AA- by Standard
& Poor’s or Fitch, Aa3 by Moody’s, or equivalent ratings from another NRSRO at the time of
purchase.

If a supranational security is downgraded below these minimum standards after purchase, the
Finance Director shall review the holding and determine whether continued ownership is
prudent and consistent with the objectives of this Investment Policy.


8.0 – Prohibited Investments
Equities (stocks), collateralized mortgage obligations, asset-backed securities, money market
mutual funds, inverse floaters, negotiable certificates of deposit, reverse repurchase agreements,
and cryptocurrency are not authorized.

Any investment type not expressly permitted in this policy is ineligible.



9.0 – Diversification and Maximum Maturities
Diversification is required to reduce overall portfolio risk while achieving market
rates of return. Diversification by issuer, security type, and maturity shall be used
to avoid over-concentration. Percentage limits will be based on market value
and will be calculated at the time of purchase (settlement date).

Except as provided below, the City will invest in securities with maturities of five
(5) years or less from the date of purchase.

                                                                                                Page 463 of 578
                                                                             CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                           Policies and Procedures




       1. The maximum weighted average maturity of the total portfolio shall not
          exceed three (3) years.
       2. The maximum duration of the corporate notes portfolio shall not exceed
          three (3) years.
       3. Callable agency securities are permitted, provided aggregate holdings
          do not exceed 35 percent of the total portfolio at the time of purchase.
       4. Liquidity funds shall be held in LGIP, bank deposits, or short-term
          instruments maturing within six (6) months.
       5. The portfolio will maintain securities maturing between one (1) day and
          five (5) years.
       6. Investments exceeding five (5) years may be permitted when matched
          to expected use of funds.

   10.0 – Downgraded Securities
   The City may, from time to time, hold securities that are downgraded below minimum policy
   standards. In such cases, the Investment Officer shall review the holding and recommend an
   appropriate course of action to the City Manager.


   If an Investment Advisor is utilized, the Advisor shall notify the Investment Officer and provide
   recommendations within one month.


   The City may continue to hold a downgraded security to maturity if doing so is determined to be
   in the best interest of the City and consistent with preservation of capital and avoidance of
   unnecessary realized losses.


   11.0 – Collateralization
      •   Depository Collateral. State statute (RCW 39.58) requires that all deposits of public funds
          be made with qualified public depositaries, protected through the actions of the Public
          Deposit Protection Commission (PDPC), comprised of the State Treasurer, Governor and
          Lieutenant Governor. State law requires that all deposits of public funds over and above
          federally insured amounts (including Certificates of Deposit) be collateralized in
          accordance with regulations of the PDPC. All collateral is regulated by the PDPC. The PDPC
          ensures public funds deposited in banks are protected should a financial institution
          become insolvent.



                                                                                                  11




                                                                                                Page 465 of 578
                                                                             CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                           Policies and Procedures



   •   Repurchase Agreements. The collateral for repurchase agreements shall be U.S. Treasury
       or Agency securities with a term of maturity not to exceed the maximum maturity allowed
       by investment policy. Mortgage-backed securities of any maturity will not be accepted as
       collateral. In order to anticipate market changes and provide a level of security for all funds,
       the collateralization level will be at 102% of market value of principal and accrued interest.
       Collateral is to be delivered to and held by the trust department of the bank with whom
       the Treasurer is currently using as the City’s safekeeping custodian. Collateral held for
       repurchase agreements will be evidenced by safekeeping receipts provided to the
       Investment Officer.


12.0 – Safekeeping and Custody
Security transactions entered into by the City shall be conducted on a delivery-versus-payment
(DVP) basis. Securities will be held by a third-party custodian designated by the Finance Director,
or his/her designee, and evidenced by safekeeping reports which will be reconciled monthly to
the portfolio. Third-party custodial reports shall be required monthly, to list, at a minimum, each
individual security, CUSIP, purchase date, cost, market value, par value, and maturity date.


13.0 – Performance Standards / Benchmarks
The City’s investment portfolio will be designed to obtain a market average rate of return during
budgetary and economic cycles, taking into account the City's investment risk constraints and
cash flow needs. Appropriate benchmarks shall be established against which portfolio
performance shall be compared on a regular basis. The benchmarks shall be reflective of the actual
securities being purchased and a comparison to the LGIP earnings rate should be completed on
a regular basis.


14.0 – Reporting and Disclosure
Monthly Reports. The Investment Officer shall make a monthly report of all treasury activity to
the City Council (RCW 35.39.032). The treasury report should provide a summary of the current
investment portfolio and the individual transactions executed to show holdings and activities
during the reporting period conform to the investment policy. The report should include the
following:

   •   An asset listing showing par value, cost and market value, type of investment, issuer, days
       to maturity and interest rate of each security;
   •   Average days to maturity of the portfolio;
   •   Maturity distribution of the portfolio and distribution by type of investment.
   •   Credit quality of portfolio holdings;
                                                                                                    12




                                                                                                  Page 466 of 578
                                                                         CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                       Policies and Procedures



   •   Average weighted yield to maturity of portfolio on investments; and,
   •   Performance comparison to benchmark


15.0 – Internal Controls
The Office of the State Auditor requires that in accordance with Revised Code of Washington
43.09.260, the City must undergo annual financial examinations performed by State Examiners.
Investment management is to be included as part of the annual independent audit to ensure
compliance with this investment policy.
The City's internal controls shall be designed to prevent losses of public funds arising from
fraud, employee error, misrepresentation by third parties, or unanticipated changes in financial
markets. Controls which the City deems important include, but are not limited to:
    • Control of collusion
    • Separation of functions
    • Separation of transaction authority from accounting and recordkeeping
    • Custodial safekeeping
    • Avoidance of bearer-form securities
    • Specific limitations regarding securities losses and remedial action
    • Clear delegation of authority to subordinate staff members
    • Written confirmation of telephone transactions
    • Supervisory authority of employee actions
    • Minimize the number of authorized investment officials
    • Documentation of transactions and strategies


16.0 – Review, Approval and Adoption
This investment policy shall be adopted by resolution of the City Council. The policy shall be
reviewed annually by the Investment Officer, and any significant modifications must be approved
by resolution.


17.0 – State and Federal Amendments
If new legislation or regulation should amend the permitted instruments or institutions, those
changes will be deemed to be immediately incorporated into this policy.


18.0 – Glossary
Agency – A debt security issued by a federal or federally sponsored agency. Federal agencies are
backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. Government. Federally Sponsored Agencies (FSAs)
                                                                                               13




                                                                                             Page 467 of 578
                                                                          CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                        Policies and Procedures



are backed by each particular agency with a market perception that there is an implicit
government guarantee. (Also see FEDERAL AGENCY SECURITIES and GOVERNMENT SECURITY)

Amortization – In portfolio accounting, periodic charges made against interest income on
premium bonds in anticipation of receipt of the call price at call or of par value at maturity.

Average Maturity – A weighted average of the expiration dates for a portfolio of debt securities.
An income fund's volatility can be managed by shortening or lengthening the average maturity
of its portfolio.

Bond – A long-term debt security, or IOU, issued by a government or corporation that generally
pays a stated rate of interest and returns the face value on the maturity date.

Book Entry Securities – U.S. government and federal agency securities that do not exist in
definitive (paper) form; they exist only in computerized files maintained by the Federal Reserve
Bank.

Book Value – The amount at which an asset is carried on the books of the owner. The book value
of an asset does not necessarily have a significant relationship to market value.

Broker – A broker brings buyers and sellers together for a commission paid by the initiator of the
transaction or by both sides.

Bullet – Non-callable. The investment can be held to maturity without concern that it will be
called. [propose adding]

Callable – An investment that the issuer has the right to redeem, or buy back, the security at a
call date or a during a range of call dates. [propose adding]

Certificates of Deposit – Certificates of Deposit, familiarly known as CDs, are certificates issued
against funds deposited in a bank for a definite period of time and earning a specified rate of
return.

Collateral – Property (as securities) pledged by a borrower to protect the interest of the lender.

Commercial Paper – An unsecured short-term promise to repay a fixed amount on a certain
future date. Commercial paper usually matures from 2 to 270 days and is traded on a discount
basis. This debt instrument, issued by banks, companies and other borrowers, uses only their credit
ratings to back the security.



                                                                                                 14




                                                                                              Page 468 of 578
                                                                              CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                            Policies and Procedures



Corporate Bond/Note – A debt security issued by a corporation. The backing for the bond is
usually the payment ability of the company, which is typically money to be earned from future
operations. Corporate bonds are considered higher risk than government bonds. As a result,
interest rates are almost always higher, even for higher credit quality companies. Most corporate
bonds have maturities greater than one year. Corporate debt that matures in less than one year
is typically called commercial paper.

Credit Quality – The measurement of the financial strength of a bond issuer. This measurement
helps an investor to understand an issuer’s ability to make timely interest payments and repay the
loan principal upon maturity. Generally, the higher the credit quality of a bond issuer, the lower
the interest rate paid by the issuer because the risk of default is lower. Credit quality ratings are
provided by nationally recognized rating agencies.

Credit Risk – The risk that another party to an investment transaction will not fulfill its obligations.
Credit risk can be associated with the issuer of a security, a financial institution holding the entity's
deposit, or a third-party holding securities or collateral. Credit risk exposure can be affected by a
concentration of deposits or investments in any one investment type or with any one party.

Cryptocurrency – A digital currency verified by a decentralized system using cryptography,
outside a centralized government or authority; a foreign currency with no country.

Custodian – An independent third party (usually bank or trust company) that holds securities in
safekeeping as an agent for the city. Also known as safekeeping.

Dealer – A dealer, as opposed to a broker, acts as a principal in all transactions, buying and selling
for his own account.

Delivery – The providing of a security in an acceptable form to the City or to an agent acting on
behalf of the City and independent of the seller. Acceptable forms can be physical securities or
the transfer of book entry securities. The important distinction is that the transfer accomplishes
absolute ownership control by the City

Delivery vs. Payment (DVP) – There are two methods of delivery of securities: Delivery vs.
payment and delivery vs. receipt (also called free). Delivery vs. payment is delivery of securities
with an exchange of money for the securities. Delivery vs. receipt is delivery of securities with an
exchange of a signed receipt for the securities.

Depository bank – A bank used as the point of deposit for cash receipts.

Depository Insurance – Insurance on deposits with financial institutions. For purposes of this
policy statement, depository insurance includes a) Federal depository insurance funds, such as

                                                                                                      15




                                                                                                    Page 469 of 578
                                                                           CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                         Policies and Procedures



those maintained by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) AND Federal Savings and
Loan Insurance Corporation (FSLIC); and b) Public Deposit Protection Commission.


Discount – 1. (n.) selling below par; e.g., a $1,000 bond selling for $900. 2. (v.) anticipating the
effects of news on a security's value; e.g., “The market had already discounted the effect of the
labor strike by bidding the company's stock down."

Diversification – Dividing available funds among a variety of securities and institutions so as to
minimize market risk.

Divestment – Conversion into cash. Divestment. Sale. Liquidation.

Face Value – The value of a bond stated on the bond certificate; thus, the redemption value at
maturity. Most bonds have a face value, or par, of $1,000.

Federal Agency Securities – Several government-sponsored agencies, in recent years, have
issued short and long-term notes. Such notes typically are issued through dealers, mostly
investment banking houses. These Federal government-sponsored agencies were established by
the U.S. Congress to undertake various types of financing without tapping the public treasury. In
order to do so, the agencies have been given the power to borrow money by issuing securities,
generally under the authority of an act of Congress. These securities are highly acceptable and
marketable for several reasons, mainly because they are exempt from state, municipal and local
income taxes. Furthermore, agency securities must offer a higher yield than direct Treasury debt
of the same maturity to find investors, partly because these securities are not direct obligations
of the Treasury.

The main agency borrowing institutions are the Federal National Mortgage Association (FNMA),
the Federal Home Loan Bank System (FHLB), and the Federal Farm Credit Bank System (FFCB).

Federal Deposit Insurance Corp (FDIC) – A Federal institution that insures bank deposits. The
current limit is up to $250,000 per depository account.

Federal Farm Credit Bank – FFCB – The Farm Credit System is a nationwide network of borrower-
owned lending institutions and specialized service organizations. Established by Congress in 1916
as the authority for certain predecessor entities, the System is the oldest of the Government-
sponsored enterprises. Throughout its long history, the fundamental purpose of the System has
remained the same: To provide American agriculture with sound and dependable credit at
competitive interest rates. Currently, there are three Farm Credit Banks and one Agricultural Credit
Bank providing funds and support services to approximately 78 locally owned Farm Credit


                                                                                                 16




                                                                                               Page 470 of 578
                                                                           CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                         Policies and Procedures



Associations and numerous cooperatives nationwide. Approximately 40 percent of the real estate
and non-real estate credit needs of U.S. agriculture are met by the System

Federal Home Loan Bank – FHLB – Created by the Federal Home Loan Bank Act of 1932 to
increase the amount of funds available for lending institutions who provide mortgages and similar
loan agreements to individuals. Having served its original objectives well, the FHLB system now
primarily focuses on increasing the amount of loanable funds available for affordable housing and
community development projects. It continues to have a material impact on housing and
development financing offering funds to member institutions at rates that are usually lower than
commercially competitive prices. The 11 banks of the FHLB Bank System are owned by over 7,300
regulated financial institutions from all 50 states, U.S. possessions, and territories.

Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation – FHLMC (Freddie Mac) – Is a stockholder-owned,
government-sponsored enterprise chartered by Congress in 1970 to keep money flowing to
mortgage lenders in support of homeownership and rental housing for middle income Americans.
FHLMC purchases, guarantees and securitizes mortgages to form mortgage-backed securities.
The mortgage-backed securities that it issues tend to be very liquid and carry a credit rating close
to that of U.S. Treasuries.

Federal National Mortgage Association – FNMA (Fannie Mae) – FNMA, like GNMA, was
chartered under the Federal National Mortgage Association Act in 1938. FNMA is a Federal
corporation working under the auspices of the Department of Housing and Urban Development,
HUD. It is the largest single provider of residential mortgage funds in the United States. Fannie
Mae, as the corporation is called, is a private stockholder-owned corporation. The corporation's
purchases include a variety of adjustable mortgages and second loans, in addition to fixed-rate
mortgages. FNMA's securities are also highly liquid and are widely accepted. FNMA assumes and
guarantees that all security holders will receive timely payment of principal and interest.

Financial Institutions – Establishments that include the circulation of money, the granting of
credit, the making of investments, and the provision of banking facilities.

FINRA – Financial Industry Regulatory Authority - a self-regulatory organization authorized to
regulate U.S. stockbrokers and broker-dealer firms. Brokers must be registered with FINRA in order
to execute trades on behalf of their clients.

Fiscal Agency – A financial institution that handles certain bond and coupon redemptions on
behalf of the entity.

Government Security – Any debt obligation issued by the U.S. government, its agencies or
instrumentalities. Certain securities, such as Treasury Bonds and GNMA’s, are backed by the


                                                                                                 17




                                                                                               Page 471 of 578
                                                                            CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                          Policies and Procedures



government as to both principal and interest payments. Other securities, such as those issued by
the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, are backed by the issuing agency.

Liquidity – Refers to the ease and speed with which an asset can be converted into cash without
a substantial loss in value.

Loss – The excess of the cost or book value of an asset over selling price.

Local Government Investment Pool (LGIP) – The aggregate of all funds from political
subdivisions that are placed in the custody of the State Treasurer for investment and reinvestment.

Mark-to-market – An adjustment in the valuation of a securities portfolio to reflect the current
market values of the respective securities in the portfolio.

Marketability – Ability to sell quickly and at competitive prices.

Market Risk – The risk associated with declines or rises in interest rates which cause an investment
in a fixed-income security to increase or decrease in value. The risk that the market value of an
investment, collateral protecting a deposit, or securities underlying a repurchase agreement will
decline.

Market Value – The price at which a security is trading and could be sold.

Master Repurchase Agreement – An agreement between the investor and the dealer or financial
institution. This agreement defines the nature of the transactions, identifies the relationship
between the parties, establishes normal practices regarding ownership and custody of the
collateral securities during the term of the investment, provides for remedies in the event of a
default by either party and otherwise clarifies issues of ownership.

Maturity – The time when a security becomes due and at which time the principal and interest or
final coupon payment is paid to the investor.

Nationally Recognized Statistical Rating Organization (NRSRO) – A credit rating agency that
issues credit ratings that the U. S Securities and Exchange Commission permits other financial
firms to use for certain regulatory purposes (i.e. Fitch, Moody’s S&P).

Net Worth – A financial institutions available funds after their total liabilities have been deducted
from their total assets.

Par Value – The nominal or face value of a debt security; that is, the value at maturity.


                                                                                                  18




                                                                                                Page 472 of 578
                                                                           CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                         Policies and Procedures



Portfolio – Collection of securities held by an investor.

Premium – The amount by which a bond sells above its par value.

Primary Dealers – A pre-approved bank, broker/dealer or other financial institution that is able
to make business deals with the U.S. Federal Reserve, such as underwriting new government debt.
These dealers must meet certain liquidity requirements as well as provide a valuable flow of
information to the Fed about the state of the worldwide markets.

Principal – An invested amount on which interest is charged or earned.

Prudence – The ability to govern and discipline oneself by the use of reason. Shrewdness in the
management of affairs. Able to use skill and good judgment in the use of resources.

Public Fund Interest-bearing Investment Accounts – Bank accounts with Qualified Public
Depositories which pay a rate of interest on the balance maintained. Used in diversifying the
investment portfolio and most commonly used as part of a liquidity portfolio.

Qualified Public Depository – A financial institution which does not claim exemption from the
payment of any sales or compensating use or ad valorem taxes under the laws of this state, which
has segregated, for the benefit of the commission, eligible collateral having a value of not less
than its maximum liability and which has been approved by the Public Deposit Protection
Commission to hold public deposits.

Repurchase Agreement (Repo) – The Repo is a contractual transaction between an investor and
an issuing financial institution (not a secured loan). The investor exchanges cash for temporary
ownership of specific securities, with an agreement between the parties that on a future date, the
financial institution will repurchase the securities at a prearranged price. An "Open Repo" does
not have a specified repurchase date and the repurchase price is established by a formula
computation.

Reverse Repurchase Agreement (Reverse Repo) – The opposite of the transaction undertaken
through a regular repurchase agreement. In a "reverse" the City initially owns securities and the
bank or dealer temporarily exchanges cash for this collateral. This is, in effect, temporarily
borrowing cash at a high interest rate and is also known as securities lending. Most typically, a
Repo is initiated by the lender of funds. Reverses are used by dealers to borrow securities they
have shorted.

Safekeeping – A service to customers rendered by banks for a fee whereby all securities and
valuables of all types and descriptions are held in the bank's vaults for protection, or in the case


                                                                                                 19




                                                                                               Page 473 of 578
                                                                            CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                          Policies and Procedures



of book entry securities, are held and recorded in the customer's name and are inaccessible to
anyone else.

Securities – Bonds, notes, mortgages, or other forms of negotiable or non-negotiable
instruments.

Securities and Exchange Commission – (SEC) – A U.S. government agency that oversees
securities transactions, activities of financial professionals and mutual fund trading to prevent
fraud and intentional deception. The SEC consists of five commissioners who serve staggered five-
year terms. No more than three of the commissioners may belong to the same political party.

Settlement Date – The day on which payment is due for a securities purchase. For stocks and
mutual funds bought through an investment dealer, settlement is normally five business days after
the trade date. Bonds and options normally settle one business day after the trade date mutual
fund shares purchased directly by mail or wire settle on the day payment is received.

Supranational Institution (SUPRA) – An international organization, or union, whereby member
states transcend national boundaries or interests to share in the decision making and vote on
issues pertaining to the wider grouping. It is formed by two or more central governments through
international treaties. The purpose for creating a supranational is to promote economic
development for the member countries. The International Bank for Reconstruction and
Development (World Bank), the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB), IFC (International
Finance Corporation) and ADB (Asian Development Bank) are examples of supra’s.

Tripartite Custodian Agreement – An agreement that occurs when a third party or custodian
becomes a direct participant in a repurchase transaction. The custodian ensures that the exchange
occurs simultaneously and that appropriate safeguards are in place to protect the investor’s
interest in the underlying collateral.

Third-party Safekeeping – A safekeeping arrangement whereby the investor has full control over
the securities being held and the dealer or bank investment department has no access to the
securities being held.

Time Deposit – Interest-bearing deposit at a savings institution that has a specific maturity.

Treasury Bills (commonly called "T-Bills ) - Treasury Bills are short-term debt obligations of the
U.S. Government. They offer maximum safety of principal since they are backed by the full faith
and credit of the United States Government. T-Bills are sold in three, six, nine, and twelve-month
bills. Because Treasury Bills are considered "risk-free," these instruments generally yield the lowest
returns in the major money market instruments.


                                                                                                   20




                                                                                                 Page 474 of 578
                                                                             CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                           Policies and Procedures



Treasury Notes and Bonds – While T-Bills are sold at a discount rate that establishes the yield to
maturity, all other marketable treasury obligations are coupon issued. These include Treasury
Notes with maturities from one to ten years and Treasury Bonds with maturities of 10-30 years.
The instruments are typically held by banks and savings and loan associations. Since Bills, Notes
and Bonds are general obligations of the U.S. Government, and since the Federal Government has
the lowest credit risk of all participants in the money market, its obligations generally offer a lower
yield to the investor than do other securities of comparable maturities.

Underlying Securities – Future securities transferred, the object of a repurchase agreement.

Vendor – A business or individual who provides a service or product at a cost.

Yield – The rate at which an investment pays out interest or dividend income, expressed in
percentage terms and calculated by dividing the amount paid by the price of the security and
annualizing the result.

Subject
Resolution Amending the City's Financial Policies for 2027-2028

Key Points

     • Over the years, the City has developed Financial Policies to guide the budget development
       process.
     • As a practice, the City amends the Financial Policies as part of its biennial budget process.
     • The Financial Policies establish a framework to build the City's financial future and ensure best
       practices to ensure long-term fiscal stability.
     • The Financial Policies for 2027-2028 were reviewed through a new leadership lens with the
       objectives of movement towards modernizing the policies to reflect the current economic and
       fiscal environment, and that they are realistic, achievable and tailored to the needs of the City.


Strategic Plan Alignment
High Performing Government – a government that is reliable, fiscally responsible, equitable, and
open to compromise.

Present Situation
The City Council, as part of the budget adoption process, approves the City's financial policies, which
establish the framework to build the City's financial future. Financial policies ensure best practices to
ensure long-term stability, as well as simplify and modernize practices to reflect the current fiscal
environment. Every biennium, it is good practice to review the financial policies to ensure they are
realistic, achievable, and tailored to the City. Every jurisdiction is unique, and financial policies are not
meant to be a one-size-fits-all approach. Additionally, with the change in city leadership of the new
City Manager, Lon Pluckhahn, and a few new directors since the last budget, a review of the financial
policies looking through a new leadership lens is good practice.

During this biennium, as shared during the August 24 workshop, there are more changes to the
financial policies than in the past due to some larger themes: updating for accessibility, addressing
the need for debt service for upcoming capital projects such as the Public Works Operations Campus,
and a review of the policies in general with new leadership. Additionally, there are updates on
language usage for equity, creation of new capital improvement plans, and commitments by specific
departments to finalize their respective cost recovery analyses.

Among the changes within the financial policies, two specific changes to highlight are: a) a new
formula for Compensated Absences Reserve fund balance to an average of a five-year actual usage
of paid-time off from the General, Street and Fire funds multiplied by 150%; and, b) changing the

                                                                                                 Page 476 of 578
designation of $1M in the Designated Reserve from the Columbia Arts Center to the Arts Hub Project.

Advantage(s)
Updates the City Financial Policies for emerging issues and practices.

Challenge(s)
None

Budget Impact
The 2027-2028 Biennial Budget is built on the framework outline in the Financial Policies.

    • Council Workshop, Financial Policies and Investment Policy Update - August 24, 2026

Purpose: In addition to following all laws related to budgeting as outlined by the
Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 35, the City has internal Financial Management
Policies that are adopted by the City Council and reviewed every two years during the
budget development process.
Policy Statement: The City Financial Policies are a compendium of all city policies that
shape the budget and ensure that the City maintains a healthy financial foundation
while planning for the future. The goal of these policies is to promote:
   •   An extended six-year financial planning horizon in alignment with the City’s
       Strategic Plan to increase awareness of future potential challenges and
       opportunities.
   •   Setting aside reserves for contingencies, replacement of capital equipment and
       other similar needs.
   •   Maintaining the effective buying power of fees and charges and modifying cost
       recovery targets when appropriate.
   •   Accountability for meeting standards of financial management and efficiency in
       providing services.
   •   Management of the City’s physical assets to provide sustainable service levels
       into the future.
   •   Planning for the capital needs of public facilities for the community and
       managing them for future use.
   •   Improved equity for those we serve through investments and revenue structures.




RESOLUTION - 5




                                                                                       Page 482 of 578
                                                               CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                 Policies and Procedures

   •   An emphasis on improving community safety through strategic deployment of the
       City’s financial resources.
   •   Improving the City’s overall impact on climate change through strategic
       investments in infrastructure and integrating climate change goals into new
       capital projects and renovation and/or remodels of existing facilities wherever
       possible.
   •   Ensuring quality bond ratings through strategic debt strategies.
   •   Investing public funds to provide maximum security with appropriate returns and
       timely liquidity.
   •   Investment of public funds in accordance with the City’s Investment Policy.
   •   Communication to the community regarding how the City’s Strategic Plan goals
       are being addressed.

1.0 Long-Range Financial Planning and Resource Utilization
It is essential for the City to incorporate a long-term perspective and monitor the
performance of programs competing to receive funding. Management will ensure
compliance with the legally adopted budget. Purchases and expenditures will comply
with legal requirements and policies and procedures set forth by the City.
   1. A long-term forecast of revenues and expenditures will be developed for all
      operating funds for the six-year period following the end of the current biennial
      budget.




RESOLUTION - 6




                                                                                     Page 483 of 578
                                                              CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                 Policies and Procedures

   2. The financial impact of budget decisions made during the development of the
      biennial budget will be reviewed in the context of the six-year forecast.

   3. The operating budget will be based on the principle that current operating
      expenditures, including debt service, will be funded with current revenues. The
      budget will not use one-time (non-recurring) sources to fund ongoing (recurring)
      uses for more than one biennium, postpone expenditures, or use internal
      borrowing to fund operations. Pausing current expenditures may occur as
      evaluation of programs are conducted. The budget will incorporate the best
      available estimates of revenues and expenditures.

   4. The City aspires toward the use of performance management and will be utilized
      as part of the budget prioritization to ensure alignment with the City’s goals and
      strategic commitments. Wherever possible, performance data will be used to
      support budgetary decisions. Measures should be developed to reflect the City’s
      efficiency and effectiveness. Status of key performance updates will be reported
      to the Council.

   5. Positive progress towards climate action, equity and inclusion and community
      safety will be measured annually. Equity and environmental sustainability lenses
      will be developed and utilized to support budgetary decisions. Status of key
      performance measures will be reported to the City Council annually.

   6. Service levels will be defined and measured in a manner that is based on results,
      including improving equity, safety and advancing climate action goals in the
      community (e.g., units of service delivered, service quality and customer
      satisfaction) rather than resources allocated to provide the service and shall be
      considered in development of the Biennial Budget.

   7. The City will endeavor to maintain a diversified general revenue base to diminish
      the effects of short-term fluctuations on any given revenue. The goal is to have a
      combination of revenues that grow in response to a good economy and those
      that remain stable during times of economic downturn. Examples of the former
      include sales taxes, utility taxes and building permit fees. Examples of the latter
      include property taxes, court fine revenues, and gambling tax.
