2.0 Reserves
Reserves are an important indicator of the City’s financial position and its ability to
withstand adverse events. Detailed policies pertaining to fund balance classifications
can be found in the City’s Fund Balance Policy. Maintaining reserves is a prudent
management practice.
   1. An emergency General Fund reserve, will be maintained equal to 7% of actual
      external revenues in the preceding fiscal year in the General, Street and Fire
      Funds. The emergency reserve is for unexpected, large-scale events where
      damage in excess of $1 million is incurred and immediate, remedial action must
      be taken to protect the health and safety of the community and continuity of city
      operations (e.g., major flood and earthquake, other natural disaster, cybersecurity
      event, pandemic, infrastructure collapse, city facility failure). Remedial actions
      include, but are not limited to funding medical supplies, temporary clinics, and
      disease-control efforts, strengthening first responders and evacuation systems;
      repairing critical infrastructure like power, water roads, bridges, citywide
      information technology infrastructure, citywide facilities and related support
      services; providing shelters and essential services for vulnerable residents, and
      improving communication , coordination and preparedness through training,
      alerts and community outreach. In the event that these “emergency reserve:
      funds are used, the City shall restore the reserve to the full 7% level within a
      reasonable amount of time as necessitated by the scale of emergency. A clear
      plan will be developed to refill the reserve, and the first significant deposit will
      occur the following fiscal year after the event.

   2. The City will maintain additional working capital reserves, sufficient to fund, on
      average, of 60-90 days of operations in each city operating fund and 45 days for
      utility funds. This reserve will address cash flow requirements and allow the City
      to operate without funding its operations through short-term borrowing.

RESOLUTION - 11




                                                                                      Page 488 of 578
                                                                 CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                    Policies and Procedures


   3. The City will maintain a revenue stabilization reserve with a goal of reaching 2.5%
      of the current year’s budget in the General Fund. This reserve may be used to
      provide funding to temporarily offset unanticipated fluctuations in ongoing
      revenues or unanticipated events, such as unexpected external mandates,
      reductions in state-shared revenues, etc. The reserve funds will provide time for
      the City to restructure its operations in a deliberate manner to ensure
      continuance of critical city activities. If the reserve is spent down, it shall be
      restored within the following two years. This reserve could be utilized if there is
      an identified three-to-six-month trend of reduced revenues.

   4. An additional designated liability funding reserve will be created when the City
      accepts funding leading to future liabilities. The reserve will be equal to the
      stated liability in the future. If a federal or state grant requires local resources to
      fund the initiative after the grant expiration, the cost of funding the initiative is
      considered to be a liability that will be funded from the “designated liability
      funding reserve. The current designated liability reserve is for public
      infrastructure tied to the HP, Inc. Development Agreement.

   5. The City will set aside a compensated absences reserve to fund 150% of the
      average of the past five years’ actual leave payoff amount.

   6. The Designated Reserve exists when the City accepts funding leading to future
      liabilities. This reserve, currently designated at $4.7M, is comprised of different
      liabilities as notated in Attachment A to this Policy. An example is Council’s
      designation of reserves representing proceeds from the sale of the Columbia Arts
      Center and is redesignated to the Arts Hub Capital Project.

   7. Funds more than the reserves will be considered unassigned General Fund
      balance and could be used to fund high-priority Council-designated one-time
      purposes, which includes but is not limited to funding accumulated currently
      unfunded deferred liabilities.

   8. Equipment replacement reserves will be maintained in the equipment services
      capital fund sufficient to replace covered vehicles and heavy equipment at the
      end of their useful lives with like/similar equipment. Equipment rates will

      include a rate to accrue the estimated replacement cost over the life of the

       hired on or after that date. In addition to the pension payments, the City is also

       none on active duty.

3.0 Asset Management
Asset Management for government infrastructure refers to the integrated,
multidisciplinary process of planning, monitoring, maintaining and managing public
infrastructure assets (e.g., water system, sewer system, transportation system, property,
buildings, etc.) throughout their entire lifecycle – from design and construction to
operation, maintenance, rehabilitation and eventual decommissioning. These assets are
essential for delivering public services, supporting economic activity, and ensuring
public safety. The goals are to maximize value, extend asset life, reduce lifecycle costs
and minimize risks of failure or service disruption. Effective asset management
balances many elements such as risk of failure, criticality of the asset, cost affordability,
safety, environmental impact and level of service, among others.
1. In pursuit of an asset management strategy that prioritizes climate action, equity and
inclusion and community safety, the City will:
       a. Consider the climate action impacts of asset investments and pursue asset
          management strategies that reduce their contribution to climate change over
          time.

       b. Consider equity and the inclusionary impacts of asset management strategies
          and prioritize investments that improve equity and inclusion within the City.

       c. Consider the potential improvements to community safety associated with
          asset management strategies and prioritize investments that improve
          community safety within the City.

       d. The General Services Department will develop a maintenance and
          improvements tasks ranking by evaluating the immediate impact on safety and
          level of service against the risk of asset failure during the 2027-2028 Biennium
          and update every biennium thereafter. This protocol prevents critical
          infrastructure degradation while properly categorizing cosmetic
          enhancements.


RESOLUTION - 14




                                                                                         Page 491 of 578
                                                                 CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                    Policies and Procedures


   2. The City will strive to integrate the principles and best practices of asset
   management such as those embodied in the International Infrastructure
   Management Manual or equivalent methodology in the management of its assets.

   3. Existing asset management strategies will include full life-cycle cost analysis.
   4. Maintenance of City assets shall be addressed on a current need rather than
   deferred into the future due to budgetary constraints. Relevant condition indexes,
   such as the Facility Condition Index (FCI), for facilities, will be used to weigh the cost
   of improvements and repairs to full replacement costs.



4.0 Capital Planning
Capital planning for government infrastructure refers to the systematic process of
identifying, prioritizing and funding major capital projects to maintain, upgrade and
expand public facilities and infrastructure. It ensures that limited public resources are
used efficiently to meet current and future community needs while aligning with
broader strategic and financial goals. Capital planning will, under the Asset
Management strategies, help the City prioritize projects, coordinate infrastructure needs
with land use, budgeting and economic development strategies, and help leverage
funding opportunities such as grants, low interest loans and bonds.
1. A rolling six-year city-wide Capital Improvement Program shall be developed bi-
   annually and shall provide a prioritized list of reasonably funded projects and those
   in process of securing funding. The six-year Capital Improvement Program shall be
   consistent with the current Comprehensive Plan and system-wide plans as required
   by Washington State Statutes or permits (e.g. Water System Plan Update, General
   Sewer Plan and Facilities Plan, Transportation Improvement Program, etc.), and any
   other plans adopted by the City Council.

2. The resources that support current outstanding debt on street improvement projects
   shall, once that debt is retired, be dedicated to ongoing support of the capital
   program of the City’s street fund. Eligible uses shall be consistent with the City’s
   adopted Transportation System Plan, Comprehensive Plan, and annually updated six-
   year transportation improvement program.


RESOLUTION - 15




                                                                                          Page 492 of 578
                                                              CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                 Policies and Procedures




3. Funding for capital projects, including major facilities maintenance projects, will be
   allocated in a manner consistent with asset management strategies and in a manner
   that balances community needs with city priorities, the potential for attracting
   matching funds, and the ability to reduce or limit expenses in future years.

4. The City will strive to incorporate a “pay-as-you-go” approach (using available cash
   and current resources) in the Capital Improvement Program. The Directors of
   Financial and Management Services and Public Works, working with the City
   Manager’s Office, will develop a Strategic funding Plan for Short and Long-Range
   Capital planning that utilizes a balance of tools to maximize and leverage non-
   general fund dollars whenever possible for the funding of capital improvements.
   With City Council approval, use of debt instruments may be used. Proceeds from the
   sale of city capital assets no longer utilized in operations will be deposited
   consistently with the initial ownership of the asset and invested in the highest
   priority city capital projects. Debt funding shall be considered for large capital
   projects with long useful life to better reflect inter-generational equity.

5. The biennial capital budget will be adopted at the same time as the City operating
   budget is adopted. The capital budget will include fully funded projects, as well as
   those projects notified of grant/loan funding but have not been awarded funding,

   will only contain projects identified in the Capital Improvement Program and those
   projects approved via City Council action. Capital projects may be changed through
   City Council action. General Services will develop a Capital Improvement Program

   general operating facilities and for emergency replacement of general fund
   equipment. Additions to the capital repair contingency reserve will be made based
   on council directions.

7. Impacts on net annual operating and maintenance costs will be identified as part of
   the funding considerations for new capital projects. This includes identifying
   potential reductions in maintenance costs if improvements are funded. The

5.0 Financial Asset and Liability Management
This section will be reviewed by the financial advisor and bond counsel and may return to

Investment Policies
      1. The City will invest public funds in a manner which will provide maximum
         security for the principal with the highest investment return, while meeting
         the daily cash flow demands of the City. Detailed policies are found
         separately in the City Investment Policy. The City will invest public funds in a
         manner that prioritizes the safety of principal, maintains adequate liquidity to
         meet operational needs, and achieves a market rate of return consistent with
         those objectives.
      2. The City will conform to all federal, state and local statutes governing the
         investment of public funds.

      3. All investment security transactions shall be conducted on a delivery-versus-
         payment (DVP) basis.

RESOLUTION - 17




                                                                                        Page 494 of 578
                                                               CITY OF VANCOUVER
                                                                  Policies and Procedures


      4. The City will only deposit funds with financial institutions qualified by the
         Washington Public Deposit Protection Commission and in accordance with
         the provisions of RCW 39.58.

      5. The City will issue Request for Proposals (RFPs) for banking services,
         safekeeping trust services and other contracts related to financial services.

Debt Management Policies
      1. The City will attempt pay-as-you-go financing for capital projects whenever
         practical. Debt may be used for projects with useful lives that meet or exceed
         the debt term and when it supports intergenerational equity, financial
         flexibility, or timely infrastructure delivery. The term of any debt issued shall
         not exceed the estimated useful life of the asset or project being financed.

      2. The City will issue debt in conformance with the requirements of its statutory
         general obligation debt limits. The non-voted debt limit is a sub-part of that
         limit. Revenue bonds or other debt tied to utilities or dedicated revenue
         outside the general fund are not included in the debt limit calculation. All
         debt issuances shall comply with applicable laws and statutory debt limits.
         The City will evaluate affordability, operating budget impacts, debt capacity,
         and long-term financial sustainability before issuing debt. Long-term debt will
         be issued only for capital improvements and other nonrecurring purposes and
         will not be used to fund operating expenditures.

      3. The City will reserve 10% of its non-voted debt capacity as a contingency
         against unforeseen emergencies requiring the issuance of debt. To preserve
         financial flexibility, the City will maintain a prudent margin below its statutory
         non-voted debt limit. As a policy target, outstanding non-voted general
         obligation debt should not exceed 90% of available non-voted debt capacity.

      4. The City shall not exceed 90% of the non-voted legal debt limit, excluding the
         10% reserved for emergency purposes. Debt capacity and affordability
         metrics will be reviewed annually as part of the budget and capital planning
         process.

  A RESOLUTION relating to low-income housing; providing for adoption of 2026 funding
awards for the Affordable Housing Fund and authorizing the City Manager, or his designee, to
  negotiate and execute agreements and other related documents on behalf of the City of
  Vancouver consistent with the awards; providing for Severability; and an Effective Date.

                                        Staff Report: 178-26

To:       Mayor and City Council
From:     City Manager
Date:     September 14, 2026

Subject
Resolution to Adopt Affordable Housing Fund Awards for Housing Production

Key Points

    • The Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) Admin Plan allocates $6 million annually for affordable
      housing production and preservation and $2 million annually for rental assistance.
    • Rental assistance dollars from 2026 have not been utilized and there are $5.755 million
      housing production funds available to award through 2027, plus an anticipated $6 million
      available in 2028 funds.
    • A restricted Request for Proposal (RFP) was released in July with applications from 6 existing
      awardees, as well as 2 new projects seeking an AHF commitment, received in July and
      reviewed by the Housing Advisory Committee in August.
    • The Committee and City staff are recommending awards totaling $9.5 million across 5 existing
      AHF awardees and 1 new AHF project. These awards will help release the bottleneck of
      projects that are stuck awaiting State Housing Trust Fund awards to complete their funding
      stacks.


Strategic Plan Alignment
Housing and Human Needs – meeting basic needs and partnering with organizations to support the
community

Present Situation
The Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) provides $10 million annually that can be used to support local
housing solutions. The annual allocations and eligible uses are: $6 million for rental housing
production and preservation; $2 million for rental assistance, $1 million for temporary shelter; and
$500,000 for homebuyer assistance. The remaining $500,000 is set aside for administration,
planning, project monitoring and reporting.

In recent years, housing production and preservation projects with an existing AHF award have been
stalled due to a bottleneck within the Washington State Housing Trust Fund (HTF). These projects
were counting on pairing local AHF with State HTF to achieve sufficient public subsidy to serve
tenants with very low income. However, only one project in Vancouver has received an HTF award in
the past two years, leaving a total of 564 prospective units of affordable housing with a funding gap.

The City opened a limited application for AHF housing production and preservation projects in July.

                                                                                           Page 498 of 578
The application sought to identify the financing gaps for existing AHF awardees, as well as identify
new projects seeking HTF funding that will serve priority populations. Seven applications were
received with requests totaling $20,600,000. Applications were reviewed by City staff for conformance
with underwriting criteria and evaluated by the Housing Advisory Committee. The Committee
recommended funding for six projects totaling $9,500,000. These projects represent a mix of
permanent supportive housing, family housing, and senior housing. The proposed awards utilize $7.5
million in housing production and preservation funds through 2028, plus $2 million in funds that would
be moved over from the AHF rental assistance category. The transfer of rental assistance funding to
the housing production category is recommended based on the current slow pace of spending
observed in the rental assistance category. This transfer will be evaluated annually and may be
adjusted based on spending patterns going forward.

The recommended awards are expected to support the creation of 403 affordable rental units,
including 135 AHF units. All projects serve households earning 30–60% of area median income
(AMI), with a focus on seniors, people with disabilities, and households exiting homelessness.
Projects were prioritized by community need, project readiness, and project feasibility.

Five of the recommended awards support projects with an existing AHF award. The additional AHF
awards will position these projects in a way that assumes one project will receive HTF this year, and
the other projects will be able to close their remaining funding gaps with other financing sources. One
of the recommended awards is a new project proposed by Hacienda CDC (Community Development
Corporation) to build 85 units of family housing in partnership with the YWCA (Young Women's
Christian Association) Clark County. This project is seeking to apply for State funding for the first time
and needs to showcase local support to strengthen their application. Their AHF award is conditioned
upon receiving a State funding award and will expire if they do not receive HTF this year.

    3. The award of funds to the prospective Hacienda/YWCA project will enable them to show local

 AN ORDINANCE of the City of Vancouver amending Vancouver Municipal Code Chapter 8.22
 to prohibit camping and outside habitation within 1,500 feet of the City of Vancouver Bridge
Shelter Property; amending VMC 8.22.030 “Definitions,” and VMC 8.22.040 “Unlawful Camping
       and Outside Habitation;” providing for severability and setting an effective date.

                                       Staff Report: 179-26

To:      Mayor and City Council
From:    City Manager
Date:    September 14, 2026

Subject
Amendment to Vancouver Municipal Code 8.22 Establishing a Camping and Outside Habitation
Impact Area Around the City of Vancouver Bridge Shelter

Key Points

    • The City-owned Bridge Shelter is expected to open in November 2026 and will provide 120
      temporary shelter beds along with on-site treatment and services intended to help people
      stabilize and move toward housing or other next steps.
    • VMC 8.22 currently prohibits camping and outside habitation at all times within designated
      camping and outside habitation impact areas, including areas within 1,000 feet of a Safe Stay
      Community. The Bridge Shelter is not a Safe Stay Community and is therefore not covered by
      that existing buffer.
    • The proposed ordinance amendment defines the Bridge Shelter and Bridge Shelter Property in
      Vancouver Municipal Code (VMC) 8.22.030 and amends VMC 8.22.040(B) to designate any
      area within 1,500 feet of the nearest point of the property as a “camping and outside habitation
      impact area.”
    • The proposed 1,500-foot buffer is intended to reduce the likelihood that outdoor habitation
      becomes concentrated immediately around the Bridge Shelter, support effective shelter
      operations and access, and address existing camping conditions in the surrounding area. The
      recommended distance reflects the size and function of the Bridge Shelter, conditions specific
      to this location, and staff’s review of 1,000-, 1,500-, and 2,000-foot buffer options.


Strategic Plan Alignment
Housing and Human Needs – meeting basic needs and partnering with organizations to support the
community

Safe and Prepared Community – a safe place to live, work, learn and play

Climate and Natural Systems – environmental stewardship and efforts to address climate change to
ensure a sustainable future

High Performing Government – a government that is reliable, fiscally responsible, equitable, and
open to compromise

Present Situation

                                                                                           Page 509 of 578
The City is preparing to open the Bridge Shelter at 5313 NE 94th Ave. The facility will provide 120
temporary shelter beds and co-located services for adults experiencing homelessness. Unlike the
City’s Safe Stay Communities, which consist of smaller individual shelter units and are expressly
defined and addressed in VMC Chapter 8.22, the Bridge Shelter is a congregate shelter and does not
fall within the code’s definition of a Safe Stay Community.

VMC 8.22.040 currently identifies specific impact areas where camping and outside habitation are
prohibited at all times. These include areas within 1,000 feet of a Safe Stay Community; land used to
operate public water, wastewater or stormwater facilities; areas within 200 feet of specified
waterways; and designated portions of the Burnt Bridge Creek drainage area. Outside those impact
areas, the chapter’s general time, place, and manner restrictions remain in effect.

The City’s existing Safe Stay Community buffers were established in response to the practical
relationship between shelter operations and unsheltered homelessness in the immediately
surrounding area. The City has experienced concentrations of camping or outside habitation near
some shelter and other homeless-service locations, including people seeking shelter or services or
remaining connected to people using those facilities. Establishing a defined area where camping and
outside habitation are not permitted helps prevent the area immediately surrounding a shelter from
becoming a de facto outdoor continuation or overflow of the shelter population and activity and
supports effective access, operations, outreach and site management within City shelter facilities.

Those considerations are particularly relevant at the Bridge Shelter location. The Bridge Shelter will
provide 120 beds and multiple on-site services, substantially increasing shelter capacity at one
location. Significant camping also currently occurs at several nearby locations, many of which are on
multiple Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT)-owned rights-of-way/properties,
and another approximately 70-bed shelter operates within 1,000 feet of the Bridge Shelter. The
proposed buffer is intended to reduce the likelihood that existing or displaced camping becomes
concentrated in the area(s) around or adjacent to the new facility as it begins operating.

Staff evaluated buffer distances of 1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 feet. A 1,000-foot buffer would not
encompass several nearby locations where significant camping and outside habitation currently
occurs. Extending the buffer to 1,500 feet encompasses the areas of greatest concern and provides
sufficient separation between those locations and the Bridge Shelter. A 2,000-foot buffer did not
provide a meaningful additional benefit and would further reduce the area otherwise available for
lawful nighttime camping. Staff therefore recommends a 1,500-foot buffer measured from the nearest
point of the Bridge Shelter Property.

The proposed amendment is specific to the Bridge Shelter and conditions associated with this
location. It does not establish a general buffer applicable to other land uses, change the existing
1,000-foot buffer around Safe Stay Communities, or change the general hours and locations in which
camping and outside habitation are prohibited or regulated elsewhere in the city. The restriction is
also being implemented as the City adds 120 new shelter beds. While the Bridge Shelter will not
provide sufficient capacity to shelter every person experiencing unsheltered homelessness in
Vancouver, the additional capacity significantly increases the City’s ability to offer an alternative to
living outdoors as the new geographic restriction takes effect.

Before and after the Bridge Shelter opens, HART and partner outreach agencies will continue
engaging people living unsheltered in the surrounding area and throughout the city, communicating
applicable restrictions, offering available shelter and services, and coordinating site-specific
responses consistent with the City’s overall response to unsheltered homelessness, relevant policy
and available resources.


                                                                                             Page 510 of 578
Advantage(s)

   1. Adoption would establish clear and enforceable expectations around the Bridge Shelter before
      it begins operating.
   2. The buffer would reduce the likelihood that camping and outdoor habitation becomes
      concentrated immediately around the facility, support effective shelter operations and access,
      and support the City’s commitment to mitigating impacts related to unsheltered homelessness
      around City shelter facilities and throughout the broader community.
   3. The City is simultaneously adding significant shelter capacity, creating a meaningful alternative
      to camping for many people affected by the new restriction and reducing reliance on
      enforcement or displacement alone.


Challenge(s)

   1. The amendment would reduce the public area available for lawful nighttime camping and will
      cause people currently camping within the proposed buffer who decline shelter placement to
      relocate to other locations.
   2. Implementation will require advance communication, outreach, coordination and attention to
      potential displacement impacts.
   3. Implementation may initially require additional signage or mapping, as well as outreach,
      cleanup and enforcement activity, but no material budget impact is anticipated.


Budget Impact
No budget impact is anticipated.

Prior Council Review

    • November 6, 2023 - Council Meeting
    • December 9, 2024 - Homelessness Emergency Response Update workshop
    • July 7, 2026 - Monthly Situation Report


Action Requested
On Monday, September 14, 2026, advance the ordinance amendment to VMC 8.22, establishing a
camping and outside habitation impact area around the City of Vancouver Bridge Shelter, setting the
date for the second reading and public hearing for September 21, 2026.

2,000 feet, the City Council finds that a 1,500-foot buffer reasonably addresses the identified

conditions without unnecessarily restricting additional areas otherwise available for lawful

nighttime camping and outside habitation.



        NOW, THEREFORE,

        BE IT ORDAINED BY THE CITY OF VANCOUVER:

        Section 1. Findings. The recitals set forth above, together with Staff Report ______ are

hereby incorporated by this reference as findings in support of this Ordinance.

The following definitions are applicable in this chapter unless the context otherwise requires:

“Camp” or “camping” means to pitch, create, use, or occupy camp and outside habitation facilities

for recreational purposes.

“Camp and outside habitation facilities” include, but are not limited to, tents, huts, temporary

shelters, or vehicles.

“City of Vancouver Bridge Shelter Property” means the parcel of property where the City of

“Specific population safe stay community” means a safe stay community with spaces reserved for

       A. Safe Stay Communities. Outside habitation shall be allowed at all times within safe stay

                stormwater facility;

    AN ORDINANCE relating to the 2025-26 Biennial Budget and making a supplemental
   appropriation to account for revenue in excess of initial budget projections and to meet

                                       Staff Report: 180-26

To:       Mayor and City Council
From:     City Manager
Date:     September 14, 2026

Subject
Supplemental Budget Ordinance Related to Clark County Fire District No. 5 Amended Agreement

Key Points

    • On August 24, 2026, Fire Chief Drake presented a workshop to Council outlining how seven
      support staff positions, fully funded by Fire District 5, can help advance the department’s
      strategic plan goals.
    • This proposal was previously approved by the Clark County Fire District 5 Board in April 2026.
    • A separate Council action is being heard to approve an amendment to the agreement with Fire
      District 5, which states the District will reimburse the City for these seven limited duration
      positions at 100% of actual costs through December 2029. Costs are anticipated to be
      approximately $3 million.
    • In order to move forward with the hiring of these seven limited-duration positions in the 2025-
      2026 biennium, certain adjustments to the appropriation, Full-Time Equivalent (FTE), and
      salary schedules are required by Council ordinance.


Strategic Plan Alignment
Safe and Prepared Community – a safe place to live, work, learn and play

Present Situation
The City of Vancouver and Clark County Fire District 5 (CCFD5) have maintained a cooperative fire
services agreement since 1994, which has periodically been updated by the parties. Under the terms
of the current agreement, CCFD5 funds a portion of the Vancouver Fire Department (VFD) operating
and capital costs.

In April 2026, Chief Drake presented a funding proposal to the CCFD5 Board. The proposal tied
progress on several VFD strategic plan outcomes to the addition of seven support staff at VFD. The
proposed positions are as follows:

    • 1.0 Administrative Assistant 3
    • 1.0 Data Analyst 1
    • 1.0 Fire Emergency Services Manager
    • 1.0 Fire Professional Standards Program Manager
    • 1.0 Material Control Coordinator

                                                                                          Page 523 of 578
    • 2.0 Support Specialist 2


On Monday, September 21, 2026, the Council will review the amended CCFD5 agreement with the
City of Vancouver. As part of the amended agreement, CCFD5 will reimburse 100% of actual position
costs and ancillary expenses; the CCFD5 Board has already approved this action during their April
2026 meeting.

Neither these positions nor the associated revenues and expenses were anticipated as part of the
earlier 2025-26 biennium budget actions. In order to begin implementing the agreement between the
City and Clark County Fire District 5 in the current biennium, certain City budget documents must be
amended to create additional positions and account for the additional revenue and expenses. A
supplemental budget action is needed to update the City’s total Full-Time Equivalent (FTE) count, the
Non-Union Salary Schedule, and the appropriation schedule.

Advantage(s)

    1. Approving this ordinance will allow the Fire Department to move forward with hiring seven
       limited-duration support staff. These support staff will help advance the outcomes of the Fire
       Department’s strategic plan, and support community safety.
    2. Position costs and ancillary expenses will be 100% reimbursed by Clark County Fire District 5.


Challenge(s)
Clark County Fire District 5 has agreed to fund position costs through 2029, and the Vancouver Fire
Department is establishing limited duration positions. There is no source of funds identified to retain
these positions after December 2029.

Budget Impact
The addition of 7.0 limited duration positions is expected to generate approximately $3 million in
additional costs from the 4th quarter of 2026 through December 2029. Actual position costs and
associated ancillary costs will be 100% funded by Clark County Fire District 5.

If approved, $258,408 would be added to the 2025-2026 biennium budget to support partial year
position costs.

Prior Council Review
City Council Workshop - August 24, 2026

Action Requested
On Monday, September 14, 2026, advance the ordinance, setting the date for the second reading
and public hearing for September 21, 2026.

Kathryn Shifley, Chief Financial Officer, John Drake, Fire Chief, katie.shifley@cityofvancouver.us,
John.Drake@cityofvancouver.us

                                                                                                                      Page 561 of 578
                                                        MEMORANDUM

DATE:         September 14, 2026

TO:           Mayor and Council

FROM:         Aaron Lande, Assistant City Manager
              Katherine Kelly, Policy and Program Manager

RE:           Statewide Initiatives on November 2026 Ballot

CC:           Lon Pluckhahn, City Manager


At the August 10th, 2026 Council meeting a request was made for further conversation
about two statewide initiatives that will be on the November 2026 ballot. This memo
provides summaries of both initiatives to support that Council conversation, and the full
text of both initiatives is included as attachments.

Note: Initiative summaries provided by Ballotpedia

Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 concerns parental rights relating to their children in
public school.

The ballot initiative would re-enact Initiative 2081, known as the Washington
Declaration of Parental and Legal Guardian Rights    . In 2024, the Washington State
Legislature passed the indirect initiative. However, in 2025, the legislature amended
Initiative 2081 through HB 1296, which added, modified, and repealed various provisions
from the initiative’s list of rights.

The proposed ballot initiative would re-enact the following rights, which HB 1296
repealed:
   • to receive prior notification about medical services being offered to their child,
      except in medical emergencies;
   • to receive prior notification about medical services or medications provided that
      could affect the parent’s or guardian’s health insurance costs; and




  P.O. Box 1995 | Vancouver, WA 98668-1995 | 360-487-8000 | TTY: 711 | cityofvancouver.us

                                                                                         Page 562 of 578
   •   to receive prior notification when the school arranges medical treatment that
       requires follow-up care after school hours.

The proposed ballot initiative would repeal the following rights, which HB 1296 added,
among others:
   • to have their child receive a public education in an environment where
      discrimination based on a protected class is prohibited;
   • to file a complaint on behalf of their child relating to harassment, intimidation,
      and bullying; and
   • to receive annual notice of the public school’s language access policies and
      services.

There are also several rights that the ballot initiative would re-enact that HB 1296
modified rather than repealed outright


Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 would prohibit students it defines as “biologically male”
from competing in certain school athletic activities intended for female students only. It
would require verification of biological sex by students’ healthcare providers.

The ballot initiative would require school districts and nonprofit organizations that
regulate interscholastic activities to "prohibit biologically male students from
competing with and against female students" in sports with separate team or individual
competitions for male and female students. The ballot initiative would require students
seeking to participate in athletic activities designated for female students to submit
documentation from their healthcare provider verifying "the student’s biological sex
[based on]... reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced
testosterone levels."

The Washington Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction published regulations
regarding the compliance of such statutes in public schools, specifically prohibiting
discrimination against sexual orientation including gender expression or identity  .

The initiative would change the enforcement of chapters 28A.600.200 and 28A.640.020
of the Revised Code of Washington by requiring compliance with a new section that
would prohibit biologically male students from competing with or against female
students in athletic activities that have separate classifications for male and female
students.

                                                                                        Page 563 of 578
                              INITIATIVE IL26-001




 1       AN ACT Relating to the Washington parents' bill        of   rights;
 2   amending RCW 28A.605.005; and creating new sections.


 3   BE IT ENACTED BY THE PEOPLE OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON:


 4       Sec. 1. RCW 28A.605.005 and 2025 c 369 s 501 are each amended to
 5   read as follows:
 6       (1) Subsections 2 through 5 of this section reinstate Initiative
 7   2081's laws guaranteeing parents' rights, including reviewing their
 8   children's instructional materials, accessing their school records,
 9   being notified when medical services are provided, and opting-out-of
10   certain classes. Voter approval of this initiative provides two years
11   of constitutional protection from legislative interference, which
12   reinforces Initiative 2081's laws guaranteeing parents' rights.
13       (2) The people find that: (a) Parents are the primary
14   stakeholders in their children's upbringing; (b) parental involvement
15   is a significant factor in increasing student achievement; and (c)
16   access   to   student   information    encourages   greater   parental
17   involvement.
18       (3) Parents and legal guardians of public school children younger
19   than 18 years old have all of the following rights:
20       (a) To examine the textbooks, curriculum, and supplemental
21   material used in their child's classroom;

1        AN ACT Relating to defending equity in interscholastic sports;
2    amending RCW 28A.600.200 and 28A.640.020; adding a new section to
3    chapter 28A.600 RCW; and creating new sections.


4    BE IT ENACTED BY THE PEOPLE OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON:


 5       NEW SECTION. Sec. 1. The people find:
 6       (1) Existing Washington state law and school district policies
 7   require students to undergo a routine physical examination prior to
 8   participation in interscholastic sports, which includes documentation
 9   of the student's sex assigned at birth;
10       (2) This established requirement provides a reliable and
11   medically verified basis to determine a student's biological sex;
12       (3)   Protecting   the   integrity   and   fairness   of   women's
13   interscholastic sports necessitates that students compete in athletic
14   activities consistent with the gender assigned at birth; and
15       (4) Leveraging the existing physical examination process to
16   verify biological sex ensures equity, safety, and competitive balance
17   in sports intended exclusively for female students, while respecting
18   the rights and opportunities of all participants.


19       Sec. 2. RCW 28A.600.200 and 2012 c 155 s 2 are each amended to
20   read as follows:
                                     p. 1              INITIATIVE IL26-638
                                                                    Page 573 of 578
 1        (1) Each school district board of directors is hereby granted and
 2   shall exercise the authority to control, supervise and regulate the
 3   conduct of interschool athletic activities and other interschool
 4   extracurricular activities of an athletic, cultural, social or
 5   recreational nature for students of the district. A board of
 6   directors may delegate control, supervision and regulation of any
 7   such    activity   to   the   Washington  interscholastic   activities
 8   association or any other voluntary nonprofit entity and compensate
 9   such entity for services provided, subject to the ((following))
10   conditions((:
11        (1))) outlined in this section.
12        (2) The voluntary nonprofit entity shall not discriminate in
13   connection with employment or membership upon its governing board, or
14   otherwise in connection with any function it performs, on the basis
15   of race, creed, national origin, sex or marital status((;
16       (2)(a))) (3) Any rules and policies adopted and applied by the
17   voluntary nonprofit entity that governs student participation in any
18   interschool activity shall be written((;)) and
19       (((b) Such rules and policies shall)) provide for notice of the
20   reasons and a fair opportunity to contest such reasons prior to a
21   final determination to reject a student's request to participate in
22   or to continue in an interschool activity.
23       (((3)(a))) (4) The association or other voluntary nonprofit
24   entity is authorized to impose penalties for rules violations upon
25   coaches, school district administrators, school administrators, and
26   students, as appropriate, to punish the offending party or parties((;
27       (b) No)), but no penalty may be imposed on a student or students
28   unless the student or students knowingly violated the rules or unless
29   a student gained a significant competitive advantage or materially
30   disadvantaged another student through a rule violation((;
31       (c))). Any penalty that is imposed for rules violations must be
32   proportional to the offense((;
33       (d) Any)), and any decision resulting in a penalty shall be
34   considered a decision of the school district conducting the activity
35   in which the student seeks to participate or was participating and
36   may be appealed pursuant to RCW 28A.600.205 and 28A.645.010 through
37   28A.645.030.
38       (((4))) (5) The school districts, Washington interscholastic
39   activities association districts, and leagues that participate in the
40   interschool extracurricular activities shall not impose more severe
                                     p. 2              INITIATIVE IL26-638
                                                                    Page 574 of 578
1    penalties for rule violations than can be imposed by the rules of the
2    association or the voluntary nonprofit entity.
3        (((5))) (6) Policies, procedures, rules, and other requirements
4    adopted by a school district or a voluntary nonprofit entity in
5    accordance with this section must conform with section 3 of this act.
6        (7) As used in this section and RCW 28A.600.205, "knowingly"
7    means having actual knowledge of or acting with deliberate ignorance
8    or reckless disregard for the prohibition involved.

 9       NEW SECTION. Sec. 3. A new section is added to chapter 28A.600
10   RCW to read as follows:
11       (1) Policies, procedures, rules, and other requirements adopted
12   in accordance with RCW 28A.600.200 by a school district board of
13   directors or a voluntary nonprofit entity must prohibit biologically
14   male students from competing with and against female students in
15   athletic activities with separate classifications for male and female
16   students if the athletic activity is:
17       (a) Intended for female students only; and
18       (b) An individual or team competition activity.
19       (2) A student who elects to participate in individual or team
20   competition activities intended for female students only governed
21   under subsection (1) of this section shall provide, as part of the
22   required routine sports physical examination, a health examination
23   and consent form or other statement signed by the student's personal
24   health care provider that verifies the student's biological sex,
25   relying only on one or more of the following: The student's
26   reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced
27   testosterone levels.

28       Sec. 4. RCW 28A.640.020 and 2023 c 242 s 3 are each amended to
29   read as follows:
30       (1) The superintendent of public instruction shall develop
31   regulations and guidelines to eliminate sex discrimination as it
32   applies to public school employment, counseling and guidance services
33   to students, recreational and athletic activities for students,
34   access to course offerings, and in textbooks and instructional
35   materials used by students.
36       (a) Specifically with respect to public school employment, all
37   schools shall be required to:


                                     p. 3              INITIATIVE IL26-638
                                                                   Page 575 of 578
 1        (i) Maintain credential requirements for all personnel without
 2   regard to sex;
 3       (ii) Make no differentiation in pay scale on the basis of sex;
 4       (iii) Assign school duties without regard to sex except where
 5   such assignment would involve duty in areas or situations, such as
 6   but not limited to a shower room, where persons might be disrobed;
 7        (iv) Provide the same opportunities for advancement to males and
 8   females; and
 9       (v) Make no difference in conditions of employment including, but
10   not limited to, hiring practices, leaves of absence, hours of
11   employment, and assignment of, or pay for, instructional and
12   noninstructional duties, on the basis of sex.
13       (b) Specifically with respect to counseling and guidance services
14   for students, they shall be made available to all students equally.
15   All certificated personnel shall be required to stress access to all
16   career and vocational opportunities to students without regard to
17   sex.
18       (c) Specifically with respect to recreational and athletic
19   activities, they shall be offered to all students without regard to
20   sex, except as provided in section 3 of this act. Schools may provide
21   separate teams for each sex. Schools which provide the following
22   shall do so with no disparities based on sex: Equipment and supplies;
23   medical care; services and insurance; transportation and per diem
24   allowances; opportunities to receive coaching and instruction;
25   laundry services; assignment of game officials; opportunities for
26   competition, publicity and awards; scheduling of games and practice
27   times including use of courts, gyms, and pools: PROVIDED, That such
28   scheduling of games and practice times shall be determined by local
29   administrative authorities after consideration of the public and
30   student   interest  in   attending   and  participating  in   various
31   recreational and athletic activities. Each school which provides
32   showers, toilets, or training room facilities for athletic purposes
33   shall provide comparable facilities for both sexes. Such facilities
34   may be provided either as separate facilities or shall be scheduled
35   and used separately by each sex.
36       The superintendent of public instruction shall also be required
37   to develop a student survey to distribute every three years to each
38   local school district in the state to determine student interest for
39   male/female participation in specific sports.


                                     p. 4              INITIATIVE IL26-638
                                                                   Page 576 of 578
 1       (d) Specifically with respect to course offerings, all classes
 2   shall be required to be available to all students without regard to
 3   sex: PROVIDED, That separation is permitted within any class during
 4   sessions on sex education or gym classes.
 5       (e) Specifically with respect to textbooks and instructional
 6   materials, which shall also include, but not be limited to, reference
 7   books and audiovisual materials, they shall be required to adhere to
 8   the guidelines developed by the superintendent of public instruction
 9   to implement the intent of this chapter: PROVIDED, That this
10   subsection shall not be construed to prohibit the introduction of
11   material deemed appropriate by the instructor for educational
12   purposes.
13       (2)(a) By December 31, 1994, the superintendent of public
14   instruction shall develop criteria for use by school districts in
15   developing sexual harassment policies as required under (b) of this
16   subsection. The criteria shall address the subjects of grievance
17   procedures, remedies to victims of sexual harassment, disciplinary
18   actions against violators of the policy, and other subjects at the
19   discretion of the superintendent of public instruction. Disciplinary
20   actions must conform with collective bargaining agreements and state
21   and federal laws. The superintendent of public instruction also shall
22   supply sample policies to school districts upon request.
23       (b) By June 30, 1995, every school district shall adopt and
24   implement a written policy concerning sexual harassment. The policy
25   shall apply to all school district employees, volunteers, parents,
26   and students, including, but not limited to, conduct between
27   students.
28       (c) School district policies on sexual harassment shall be
29   reviewed by the superintendent of public instruction considering the
30   criteria established under (a) of this subsection as part of the
31   monitoring process established in RCW 28A.640.030.
32       (d) The school district's sexual harassment policy shall be
33   conspicuously posted throughout each school building, and provided to
34   each employee. A copy of the policy shall appear in any publication
35   of the school or school district setting forth the rules,
36   regulations, procedures, and standards of conduct for the school or
37   school district. This requirement as it relates to students, parents,
38   and guardians may be satisfied by using the model student handbook
39   language in RCW 28A.300.286.


                                     p. 5              INITIATIVE IL26-638
                                                                   Page 577 of 578
 1       (e) Each school shall develop a process for discussing the
 2   district's sexual harassment policy. The process shall ensure the
 3   discussion addresses the definition of sexual harassment and issues
 4   covered in the sexual harassment policy.
 5       (f) "Sexual harassment" as used in this section means unwelcome
 6   sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, sexually motivated
 7   physical   contact,  or   other   verbal  or   physical   conduct  or
 8   communication of a sexual nature if:
 9       (i) Submission to that conduct or communication is made a term or
10   condition, either explicitly or implicitly, of obtaining an education
11   or employment;
12       (ii) Submission to or rejection of that conduct or communication
13   by an individual is used as a factor in decisions affecting that
14   individual's education or employment; or
15       (iii) That conduct or communication has the purpose or effect of
16   substantially interfering with an individual's educational or work
17   performance, or of creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive
18   educational or work environment.


19       NEW SECTION.   Sec. 5.   This act may be known and cited as the
20   defending equity in interscholastic sports act.


21       NEW SECTION.    Sec. 6.    If any provision of this act or its
22   application to any person or circumstance is held invalid, the
23   remainder of the act or the application of the provision to other
24   persons or circumstances is not affected.
